Of Gregory of Nyssa, Among the Saints: On the Beatitudes.

“Seeing the crowds, he went up onto the mountain; and when he had sat down, his disciples came to him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Who, then, among those gathered here is fit to be a disciple of the Word, and to go up with him from the ground, from hollow and lowly thoughts, to the spiritual mountain of lofty contemplation? This mountain has escaped every shadow cast by the hills of wickedness that rise around it. Lit on every side by the ray of the true light, it lets one look down from its height, in the clear sky of truth, on everything that is hidden from those shut in the hollow below. What things are seen from this height, and how many, God the Word himself describes as he pronounces blessed those who have gone up with him. He points them out as if with a finger: here the kingdom of heaven, there the inheritance of the land above; then mercy, and righteousness, and comfort, and kinship with the God of all; and the fruit of persecutions, which is to come to dwell with God; and whatever else may be seen besides, as the Word points from the mountain above, and as it is gazed at through hope from the [Patrol. Gr. XLIV]

lofty watchtower. Since, then, the Lord goes up onto the mountain, let us listen to Isaiah crying out: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.” Even if we are weak from sin, let us strengthen, as the prophecy directs, our drooping hands and paralysed knees. For if we reach the summit, we shall find the one who heals every disease and every infirmity, who takes up our weaknesses and bears our diseases. So let us too run toward the ascent, so that, reaching with Isaiah the ridge of hope, we may see from the height those good things which the Word shows to those who have followed him up. But may God the Word open his mouth for us as well, and teach us those things the very hearing of which is blessedness; and let the beginning of our contemplation be the beginning of the teaching we have heard. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Suppose some lover of gold came upon writings that revealed a treasure in a certain place, and the place where the treasure lay promised much sweat and toil to those who wanted to possess it. Would he lose heart before the labour, grow careless of the gain, and find it sweeter than riches to put no effort into the task? It is not so, it is not so. Rather, he will call on all his friends for this, and gathering help for himself from every quarter as best he can, he makes the hidden wealth his own by the number of hands. This, brothers, is the treasure the text reveals; but the wealth is hidden by obscurity. So let us too, who long for the incorruptible gold, make use of the many hands of prayer, so that the wealth may come into the open for us, and all may share the treasure equally, and each may possess the whole of it. For such is the way virtue is divided that it is distributed among all who lay claim to it, and is present whole to each, not diminished by those who share in it. In the distribution of earthly wealth, whoever grabs more wrongs those who have an equal share, for he who enlarges his own portion inevitably lessens that of his partner. But spiritual wealth does what the sun does: it distributes itself to all who look upon it and is present whole to each. Since, then, each hopes for an equal gain from the labour, let all contribute equally through prayer toward what we are seeking.

First, then, I say we must understand what blessedness itself is. Blessedness, by my account at least, is the sum of all that is conceived as good, from which nothing that a good desire could reach for is absent. What blessedness means may also become clearer to us if we set its opposite beside it; and the opposite of the blessed is

the wretched. Wretchedness, then, is misery amid painful and unwanted sufferings. The states of the two, arising from what befalls them, are divided as opposites. For the one who is called blessed rejoices and exults in what is set before him to enjoy, while the one who is called wretched is grieved and pained by what is present to him. What is truly blessed, then, is the Divine itself. For whatever we suppose it to be, blessedness is that incorruptible life, the unspeakable and incomprehensible good, the inexpressible beauty, grace itself, and wisdom, and power; the true light; the fountain of all goodness; the authority that transcends all things; the only thing worthy of love, which is always the same; the unending exultation; the everlasting gladness. Though one say everything he can about it, he says nothing worthy of it. For the mind does not reach what truly is, and even if we manage to conceive something loftier about it, what is conceived cannot be expressed in any word. But since the one who formed man made him in the image of God, whatever comes to be blessed by sharing in true blessedness would be called blessed in a secondary sense. For just as with bodily beauty, the original beauty is in the living, real face, and what is shown by imitation in a portrait comes second to it, so too human nature, being an image of the transcendent blessedness, is itself also marked with the beauty of the good when it displays in itself the reflections of those blessed features. But since the filth of sin had spoiled the beauty of the image, the one came who washes us in his own water, the water that is living and springs up to eternal life, so that we might put off the disgrace of sin and be renewed once more in the blessed form. And just as, in the art of painting, an expert might tell the inexperienced that a face is beautiful when it is composed of such and such features (hair of this kind, the round of the eyes, the line of the brows, the set of the cheeks, and every detail by which beauty is made complete), so the one who repaints our soul in the likeness of the only Blessed One sketches out in his words each of the features that make for blessedness, and says first: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” But what will we gain from his generosity if the meaning contained in the saying is not made plain to us? In medicine too, many precious and hard-to-obtain drugs remain useless and of no benefit to those who do not know them, until we learn from the art what each of them is good for. What, then, does it mean

to be poor in spirit, through which one comes to possess the kingdom of heaven? We have learned of two kinds of wealth from Scripture: one to be pursued and one condemned. The wealth of the virtues is to be pursued, while material and earthly wealth is decried, because the first becomes a possession of the soul, while the second is well suited to deceiving the senses. That is why the Lord forbids us to store it up, since it lies exposed to being eaten by moths and to the schemes of burglars. He bids us give our attention instead to the wealth of things on high, which the power of decay does not touch. By speaking of moth and thief, he pointed to the destroyer of the soul's treasures. If, then, poverty is the opposite of wealth, by analogy we may surely learn that poverty too is twofold: one kind to be rejected, the other called blessed. Whoever is poor in self-control, or in the precious possession of justice, or in wisdom, or in prudence, or is found needy, destitute and poor in any other of the costly treasures, is wretched in his poverty and pitiable for his lack of precious things. But whoever willingly becomes poor in everything conceived as evil, and keeps none of the devil's treasures laid up in his storerooms, but is fervent in spirit and through this stores up for himself a poverty in evils, he would be the one whom the Word points to in the poverty that is called blessed, whose fruit is the kingdom of heaven.

But let us return again to working the treasure, and not give up uncovering what is hidden by digging with our reason. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit.” It was said in a way earlier, and will be said again now, that the goal of the virtuous life is likeness to God. Yet what is free of passion and incorruptible entirely escapes human imitation, for a life subject to passions cannot possibly be made wholly like a nature that admits no passions. If, then, only the Divine is blessed, as the Apostle calls it, and men share in blessedness through likeness to God, but the imitation is impossible [?], then blessedness is beyond the reach of human life. But there are things belonging to the Godhead that are set before those who wish to imitate them as possible. What are they? It seems to me that by poverty of spirit the Word means voluntary humility. The Apostle shows us an example of this when he speaks of the poverty of God, who “though he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich.” Since, then, all the other things seen in the divine nature exceed the measure of human nature, while humility is something natural to us and bred together with us who walk on the ground, who have our being from earth and dissolve back into earth, you, by imitating God in what is natural and possible for you, have yourself put on the blessed form. And let no one suppose

that the achievement of humility costs no effort and is gained with ease. On the contrary, it is more laborious than any of the other virtues one may practise. Why? Because while the man who had received the good seed was asleep, the enemy of our life rooted in him the chief of the opposing sowing, the tare of pride. For by the very means by which the enemy hurled himself down to earth, he dragged the wretched human race down with him into a common fall; and there is no other evil to our nature like the one that comes through pride. Since, then, the passion of self-exaltation is somehow implanted in nearly everyone who shares in human nature, the Lord begins the Beatitudes here, casting pride out of our disposition as a kind of primal evil. He counsels us to imitate the one who voluntarily became poor, who is truly blessed, so that by becoming poor by choice we may be made like him as far as we are able, and so draw to ourselves a share in blessedness too. “Let this mind be in you,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus, who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave.” What could be poorer, for God, than the form of a slave? What could be lowlier, for the King of all that exists, than to enter into fellowship with our poor nature? The King of kings and Lord of lords willingly puts on the form of slavery; the Judge of all pays tribute to earthly rulers; the Lord of creation takes shelter in a cave; he who holds the universe in his grasp finds no room in the inn, but is laid aside in the manger of irrational beasts; the pure and undefiled one accepts the filth of human nature, and having passed through all our poverty, goes on to the very experience of death. See the measure of his voluntary poverty! Life tastes death; the Judge is brought to judgment; the Lord of the life of all that exists comes under a judge's verdict; the King of every power above the world does not push away the hands of the executioners. “Look to this example,” he says, “as the measure of your humility.”

Perhaps it would also be well to examine how irrational this passion is, so that the beatitude may become easy for us to attain, and humility may be achieved with great facility and ease. For just as skilled physicians master a disease more easily once they have first removed its cause, so we too, once we have checked by reason the empty vanity of the conceited, may make the road of

humility easy for ourselves to travel. How, then, could one better demonstrate the futility of conceit? How else than by showing what our nature is? For anyone who looks at himself, and not at what surrounds him, would not easily fall into such a passion. What, then, is man? Do you want me to give the more dignified and honourable account? Well, even the one who adorns our condition and dresses up human nobility in the grandest terms traces the pedigree of our nature to clay; and the nobility and dignity of the proud man is kin to brick. But if you wish to speak of the immediate and obvious origin of our birth, away with it! Do not utter a word about it, do not even mutter; do not, as the law says, uncover the nakedness of your father and mother; do not publish in speech what deserves oblivion and deep silence. And then are you not ashamed, you statue of earth, soon to be dust, carrying within you, like a bubble, a short-lived puff of air, when you are filled with pride, inflamed with conceit, and swelling your mind with vain thoughts? Do you not see both ends of human life, how it begins and in what it ends? But you pride yourself on your youth, you gaze at the bloom of your age and preen yourself on your good looks: because your hands are full of vigour for movement and your feet light for leaping; because your curls toss in the breeze and the first down outlines your cheek; because your clothes are bright with purple dye and your silken garments are embroidered with battles or hunts or scenes from stories. Or perhaps you even gaze at your shoes, carefully polished black and fancifully adorned with lines of stitching? These you look at; but do you not see yourself? I will show you, as in a mirror, who and what you are. Have you never seen the mysteries of our nature in a common burial ground? Have you not seen the heap of bones piled one on another? Skulls stripped of flesh, staring with something frightful and hideous from their empty eye sockets? Have you seen the grinning mouths, and the rest of the limbs scattered at random? If you have seen those, you have seen yourself in them. Where are the [?] of your present bloom? Where is the fresh colour of the cheek? Where is the bloom on the lip? Where is the stern beauty of the eyes, gleaming beneath the arch of the brows? Where is the straight nose that stood between the beautiful cheeks? Where is the hair on the neck? Where are the curls about the temples? Where are the hands that drew the bow, the feet that rode the horse? The purple? The fine linen? The cloak? The belt? The shoes? The horse? The gallop? The swagger? All the things by which your conceit now grows? Tell me, where among those bones are the things that now make you so puffed up and proud? What dream is so insubstantial? What phantoms of sleep are like these? What

feeble shadow so slips from the touch as the dream of youth, which no sooner appears than it flies past? So much for those who are foolish in youth because of the immaturity of their age. But what could one say about those already settled in life, whose age is steady but whose character is unstable, and in whom the disease of pride keeps growing? They call this sickness of character “dignity.” For the most part, office and the power that comes with it become the occasion of pride. For either they suffer from it while in office, or while preparing themselves for office, or the stories told about it often fan the disease into flame again even after it has died down. And what words could get within their hearing, deafened as it is by the cries of the heralds? Who will persuade people in this state that they are no different at all from those who parade on the stage? For actors too have a skilfully carved mask put on them, and a purple robe spangled with gold, and their procession in a chariot; and yet no disease of pride comes upon them from such things. As they were in mind before going on stage, so they keep the same disposition of soul during the procession, and they are not upset when they step down from the chariot and take off the costume. But those who parade in office on the stage of life, considering neither how short it is nor what comes shortly after, are like bubbles stretched by a puff of breath: in the same way these men are swollen by the loud voice of the herald, and [take on] the form of some alien mask,

[?] the natural set of the face into something unsmiling and frightening. They also contrive a harsher voice for themselves, reshaped into something bestial so as to terrify those who hear it. They no longer stay within human bounds, but claim divine power and authority for themselves. For they believe they are masters of life and death, because, of those who are tried before them, they hand one a verdict that saves him and condemn another to death. And they do not even see who is truly master of human life, the one who fixes both the beginning and the end of existence. Yet this alone would have been enough to check their vanity: to see many rulers snatched from the very midst of their thrones on the very stage of their office and carried out to their tombs, where lamentation took the place of the heralds' voices. How, then, can one who is a stranger to his own life be master of another's? If such a man, then, is poor in spirit, looking to the one who voluntarily became poor for our sake, and considering that we share an equal dignity of nature, and does not use that deluded tragedy of office to insult those of his own kind, he is truly to be called blessed, for he has exchanged a passing humility for the kingdom of heaven. Do not reject, brother,

the other sense of poverty either, which brings about wealth in heaven. “Sell all your possessions,” he says, “and give to the poor, and come, follow me, and you will have treasure in heaven.” For such poverty seems to me not out of harmony with the poverty that is called blessed. “Look, we have left everything we had and followed you,” the disciple says to the Master; “what then will there be for us?” And what is the answer? “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Do you want to understand who is poor in spirit? It is the one who has exchanged bodily abundance for the wealth of the soul, who is poor for the sake of the spirit, who has shaken off earthly wealth like a burden, so that he may be borne upward, lifted into the air, travelling on a cloud together with God, as the Apostle says. Gold is a heavy thing; heavy is all the matter that men pursue for the sake of wealth; but virtue is something light that rises upward. Now these two are opposed to each other, heaviness and lightness. It is impossible, therefore, for anyone to become light who has nailed himself to the weight of matter. If, then, we must reach the things above, let us become poor in the things that drag us down, so that we may come to be among the things above. What the way is, the psalm teaches: “He has scattered abroad, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever and ever.” Whoever shares with the poor man will set himself in the portion of the one who became poor for our sake. The Lord became poor; so do not fear poverty yourself. But the one who became poor for our sake reigns over all creation. So if you share the poverty of the one who became poor, you will also share the reign of the one who reigns. For “blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” May we too be counted worthy of it in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

[?] Those who climb to higher places by a ladder, once they have stepped onto the first rung, are raised by it to the one above; then the second brings the climber to the third, and that one to the next, and that one to the one after it. And so the climber, always lifted from where he stands to what lies above, reaches the very top of the ascent. What do I have in view in beginning this way? It seems to me that the Beatitudes are arranged in order like rungs, each making the ascent easy for the mind by way of the others. For whoever has mounted in thought onto the first beatitude is taken up by the one that follows through a necessary sequence of ideas, even if the saying seems somewhat strange compared with the first. For perhaps the hearer will say that it is not possible, as in a series of steps, that after the kingdom of heaven the

…to receive the inheritance of the earth. Yet if the discourse had to follow the nature of things, it would have been more consistent to put the earth before heaven, since our ascent to heaven would start from there. But if we could somehow be given wings by reason and stand above the back of the heavenly vault, we would find there the earth above the heavens. It is laid up as an inheritance for those who have lived virtuously. So the beatitudes do not seem to be out of order when, in the promises God sets before us, the heavens come first and the earth after them. For everything visible, as far as bodily sense is concerned, is wholly of one kind with itself. Even if one part seems high in terms of spatial distance, it still lies below the intellectual substance. Thought cannot set foot there unless reason has first passed beyond everything that sense can reach. If that higher portion is called by the name of earth, do not be amazed. The Word comes down to the lowliness of our hearing; it was for this very reason that he came down to us, because we could not be lifted up to him. So he hands on the divine mysteries through words and names familiar to us, using the terms that ordinary human life contains. In the promise before this one, too, he called that unspeakable blessedness in heaven a kingdom. Was he pointing by that word to anything like the kingdom here below? To diadems flashing with the gleam of jewels, to bright purple robes shining sweetly on greedy eyes, to porticoes and curtains, lofty thrones, ranks of bodyguards standing in rows, and all the other theatrical trappings that people add to such a stage of life when they want to magnify the pomp of power? No. But because the name of kingdom is a great thing in this life, above almost everything people covet, he used that name to point to the goods that lie beyond. If there were anything among human beings higher than kingship, he would surely have used that name above all, to lift the hearer's soul on wings toward desire for the unspeakable blessedness. For those goods, which are beyond human sense and knowledge, could not be revealed to people by their proper names. 'Eye has not seen,' it says, 'nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man.' But so that the blessedness we hope for should not wholly escape our guessing, we hear of things beyond utterance in the measure that our lowly nature can grasp. So do not let the shared name 'earth' drag your mind back down, after the heavens, to the earth below. If the earlier beatitudes have lifted you up through the Word and you have set foot on the heavenly hope, then search out for me that earth which is not everyone's inheritance, but belongs only to those who, by the gentleness of their life,

are judged worthy of that promise. The great David seems to me to have foreseen it under the Spirit's guidance. Divine Scripture testifies that he was gentle and forbearing above all who lived in his time. By faith he already held what he hoped for when he said, 'I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.' I do not think the Prophet called this earth the land 'of the living,' since it brings forth only mortal things and dissolves back into itself every kind of creature that comes from it. He knows instead a land of the living that death has never trodden. No path of sinners has been worn there, and it has received no trace of evil. The sower of tares has not furrowed it with the plough of wickedness, and it bears no thistles and thorns. There are the waters of rest and the place of green pasture, the spring that divides into four, the vine tended by the God of all, and whatever else we hear of in riddles from the inspired teaching. Now that we have understood the high earth seen above the heavens, where the city of the King has been founded and of which glorious things have been spoken, as the Prophet says, we can no longer reasonably be surprised at the order of the beatitudes. It would not have been fitting, I think, to hold out this earth as the hope of blessing for those who, as the Apostle says, will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so will always be with the Lord. What further need of the earth below do they have, whose life [?] lifted aloft in hope? For we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord. But let us see which virtue the inheritance of that earth is offered to as a prize. 'Blessed are the gentle,' it says, 'for they shall inherit the earth.' What is gentleness? And in what respect does the Word call gentleness blessed? I do not think he means that everything done gently must equally be a virtue, if this word signifies only what is quiet and slow. Among runners the gentle one is no better than the one who hurries, and the sluggish boxer does not win the crown over his opponent. When we run for the prize of the upward call, Paul advises us to increase our speed, saying, 'So run that you may obtain it.' He himself always pressed forward with ever more vigorous motion, forgetting what lay behind. In boxing he was nimble. He watched for his adversary's attack and kept his footing sure. Armed with his fists, he did not throw his punches at something empty and insubstantial, but struck his opponent's vital parts and landed his blows on the body itself. Do you want to know what Paul's boxing was like? Look at his antagonist's wounds, look at his opponent's black eyes, look at the marks on the one he defeated. Surely

you know the opponent who wrestles against us through the flesh. Paul beats him black and blue in his boxing and scratches him with the nails of self-control. He puts his members to death with hunger, thirst, cold and nakedness. He brands him with the marks of the Lord. He conquers him in the race by leaving him behind, so that his view is not blocked by the opponent running ahead. Paul, then, is quick and nimble in his contests. David lengthens his stride as he runs at his enemies. The bridegroom in the Song is likened to a gazelle for his nimbleness, leaping over mountains and bounding over hills. Many such passages could be cited where swiftness of movement is valued above gentleness. How, then, does the Word here call gentleness blessed, as though it were an achievement? 'Blessed are the gentle,' it says, 'for they shall inherit the earth'—surely that earth which yields good fruit in abundance, is luxuriant with the tree of life, is watered by springs of spiritual gifts, and on which the true vine grows, whose husbandman, we are told, is the Father of the Lord. But the Word seems to teach a lesson like this. We slip into evil very easily, and our nature quickly tips toward the worse. Heavy bodies stay completely unmoved when it comes to going upward. But if one is dislodged from some high ridge onto the slope, it rushes down so violently, its own weight increasing its speed, that its swiftness is beyond reckoning. Since quickness in such things is harmful, its opposite must surely be blessed. That is gentleness: a settled disposition that is slow and hard to move toward such impulses of nature. Fire by nature is always moving upward and cannot be moved in the opposite direction. In the same way virtue is swift toward what is above and beyond, never slackens its speed, and is fettered against the opposite impulse. Since, then, quickness toward evil abounds in our nature, it is right that stillness in such matters should be called blessed. Quietness here becomes evidence of movement upward. It would be better, though, to make the point clear through examples from life. The movement of each person's choice is twofold, proceeding freely toward whatever seems good: one way toward self-control, the other toward licentiousness. What has been said about one particular form of virtue and vice should be understood of them all. Human character is always split between opposite impulses: anger set against forbearance, arrogance against moderation, envy against goodwill, hostility against a loving and peaceable disposition. Human life is bound up with matter, and the passions are concerned with material things. Every passion has a swift and unstoppable

drive toward getting what it wants, for matter is heavy and sinks downward. That is why the Lord does not bless those who live wholly free of passion; in a life bound up with matter it is impossible to achieve a life entirely immaterial and free of passion. Instead he calls gentleness the limit of virtue attainable in life in the flesh, and says that gentleness is enough for blessedness. He does not lay down total freedom from passion as a law for human nature. It is not the part of a just lawgiver to command what nature cannot accept. That would be like moving water creatures to live in the air, or moving creatures that breathe air [?] into the water. Law must fit the capacity that is proper and natural to us. So the beatitude enjoins moderation and gentleness, not complete freedom from passion. The one lies beyond nature; the other is achieved by virtue. If the beatitude had proposed that we be wholly unmoved by desire, the blessing would be useless and of no benefit to life. Who, joined to flesh and blood, could attain such a thing? As it is, he says that the one condemned is not the person who happens to feel desire, but the one who deliberately draws the passion to himself. Such an impulse often arises even against our will, produced by the weakness mingled with our nature. But to refuse to be swept away like a torrent by the passion's force, to stand up manfully against that state and drive the passion back by reasoning: that is the work of virtue. Blessed, then, are those who do not tip quickly toward the passionate movements of the soul but are held in check by reason. In them reason, like a bridle reining in the impulses, does not let the soul be carried off into disorder. The passion of anger shows most clearly how blessed gentleness is. Some word or deed, or the suspicion of something unpleasant, stirs up this disease. The blood boils around the heart, and the soul rises up for revenge. In the myths potions change human nature into the shapes of beasts. In the same way you can suddenly see a man turned by anger into a boar, a dog, a leopard, or some other such beast. His eye is bloodshot; his hair stands on end and bristles; his voice is harsh and grows sharper as he speaks. His tongue is numbed by the passion and cannot serve the impulses within. His lips are stiff; they cannot shape words or keep in the mouth the moisture the passion produces, but shamefully spit out foam along with his voice. So it is with his hands, so with his feet, so with the whole state of his body, each limb sharing

in the passion. Suppose one man is like this. Another looks to the beatitude and calms the disease by reasoning, with a steady gaze and a quiet voice, like a physician using his skill to treat someone behaving disgracefully in a frenzy. Comparing the two, will you not say yourself that the beastly man is pitiable and loathsome, while the gentle man, who has not been twisted along with his neighbour's vice, is blessed?

That the Word has this passion especially in view is clear from the fact that he gives us the law of gentleness right after humility. The one seems to depend on the other, and the state of humility is a kind of mother of the disposition of gentleness. If you remove pride from a person's character, the passion of anger has no occasion to arise. For those who grow angry, insult and dishonour are the cause of this sickness. But dishonour does not touch someone who has trained himself in humility. Suppose someone's reasoning has been cleansed of human illusion. He sees the worthlessness that is nature's lot: the origin from which it takes its being, and the end toward which this short and swiftly ending life is carried. He sees the filth bound up with the flesh and the poverty of our nature, which cannot sustain itself on its own without making up its lack from the abundance of the irrational creatures. He sees, besides, the griefs, mournings and calamities, and the many forms of disease to which human life is subject, from which no one is by nature exempt and free. Seeing all this precisely with the cleansed eye of the soul, he will not easily be indignant when he is denied honour. On the contrary, he will consider any honour his neighbour pays him an illusion. There is nothing in our nature that can share in honour except the soul alone, and the soul's honour does not consist in the things people seek in this world. To boast of wealth, to pride oneself on birth, to look for glory, or to think oneself above one's neighbour—these are what human honours are made of—all become the ruin and disgrace of the soul's honour. So a reasonable person would not choose to stain the purity of his soul with anything of the kind. To be disposed in this way is nothing other than to live in a deep habit of humility. Once that is achieved, anger will find no entrance into the soul. And when anger is absent, a calm and quiet life is achieved. That is nothing other than gentleness, whose end is blessedness and the inheritance of the heavenly earth, in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

We have not yet reached the summit of the mountain. We are still [?] in the foothills of these thoughts, though we have already passed two hills, led up through the beatitudes to blessed poverty and then to gentleness, which stands higher still. After these the Word leads us on to higher things and shows us, through the beatitudes, a third height next in order. We must certainly run up to it, laying aside all sluggishness and, as the Apostle says, the sin that so easily entangles us. Then, light and unencumbered when we reach the top, we may draw near in our souls to the purer light of truth. What, then, does it mean: 'Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted'? Anyone whose eyes are on the world will surely laugh and mock the saying: 'If those worn down by every calamity are called blessed in this life, it follows that those whose life is free from grief and harm are wretched.' And as he lists the kinds of calamity, he will laugh all the more. He will hold up to view the evils of widowhood and the misery of orphanhood, financial losses, shipwrecks, captivity in war, unjust verdicts in court, banishments, confiscations and disgrace. He will add the misfortunes that come from disease, such as maimings and amputations and every sort of bodily disfigurement, and any other suffering that befalls people in this life, whether it touches body or soul. He will go through all of these, thinking that by them he can show the saying that blesses mourners to be ridiculous. But we will pay little attention to those who look at the divine thoughts in a petty and lowly way. Let us try, as far as we can, to discern the wealth that lies deep in this saying. That will also make clear how great the difference is between the fleshly, earthbound mind and the lofty, heavenly one. At first sight one might suppose that the blessed mourning is the mourning over offences and sins. This would follow Paul's teaching on grief. He said that grief is not of one kind only: one kind is worldly, and the other is worked according to God. The work of worldly grief is death, while the other works salvation through repentance for those who grieve. Such a state of the soul is truly not excluded from blessedness, when the soul becomes aware of its worse condition and laments its life in vice. Think of bodily illness. When some part of the body has been paralysed by an injury, the absence of pain is a sign that the paralysed part is dead. But if some medical skill restores living sensation to the body, then both the patient and those treating him rejoice

[?] the part. They take it as proof that the condition has turned toward health that the limb has now come to feel what stings it. It is the same when, as the Apostle says, some people, having become callous, give themselves over to a life of sin. They have become truly dead and paralysed with respect to the life of virtue, and they feel nothing of what they do. But suppose the healing word touches them, as if with hot and burning remedies—I mean the grim threats of the coming judgment. It stings the heart deeply with fear of what is to come: fear of Gehenna, the unquenchable fire, the undying worm, the gnashing of teeth, the ceaseless weeping, the outer darkness, and everything of that kind. It rubs and warms like hot, sharp remedies the one who has been numbed by pleasurable passions, and brings him to feel the life he has been living. Then, by producing a painful sensation in his soul, it makes him blessed. So too Paul lashes with his words the man who had raged after his father's bed, for as long as the man remained insensible of his sin. But once the medicine of rebuke had reached him, Paul begins to comfort him as one who had already become blessed through mourning, 'lest such a one,' he says, 'be swallowed up by excessive grief.' Let this thought too be of some use to us for the life of virtue as we contemplate the beatitude before us, since sin somehow abounds in human nature, and mourning that comes from repentance has been shown to be its remedy. But it seems to me that the Word hints at something deeper than this by speaking of mourning as continuous action, and leads us to understand something beyond it. If he meant only regret for wrongdoing, it would have been more consistent to bless those who have mourned, not those who mourn continually. To compare it with the course of an illness, we call blessed those who have been healed, not those who are always under treatment. A prolonged treatment shows that the sickness continues too. There is another reason, it seems to me, not to settle on this meaning alone, as though the Word gave the blessing only to those who mourn for their sins. We shall find many who have led a blameless life, one attested by the divine voice itself for every kind of excellence. What greed was there in John? What idolatry in Elijah? What sin, small or great, does the record know of in their lives? What then? Will the saying place them outside blessedness, those who were never sick at all and never needed this remedy—I mean the mourning that comes from repentance? Would it not be absurd to think that such people are shut out from divine blessedness because they neither sinned nor healed sin by mourning? Otherwise sinning would be more honourable than living without sin—

[?] …if the grace of the Comforter has been allotted only to those who repent? For "Blessed," he says, "are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted." So then, following as far as we can the One who, as Habakkuk says, sets us upon the heights, let us search once more for the meaning that lies in these words, so that we may learn to what kind of mourning the comfort of the Holy Spirit is offered. Let us consider, then, in human life, what mourning itself is in the first place, and what gives rise to it. Now this much is plain to everyone: mourning is a gloomy disposition of the soul, arising from the loss of something it holds dear, and it has no place among those who live in good cheer. Suppose, for instance, that someone prospers in life. Everything flows along pleasantly for him; he delights in his wife, rejoices in his children, is fortified by the support of his brothers; he is respected in the marketplace, honored by those in power, feared by his opponents, not despised by those under him, approachable to his friends, abounding in wealth, given to enjoyment, pleasant, free from grief, strong in body. He has everything that is thought honorable in this world, and such a man surely lives in gladness, delighting in each of the things he has. But if some reversal of his prosperity should overtake him through some evil chance, bringing separation from those dearest to him, or the loss of his possessions, or some impairment of his bodily well-being, then, with the removal of what gladdened him, the opposite disposition arises, which we call mourning. So the account given of it is true: mourning is a painful sense of the loss of what gladdens us. Now that we have understood human mourning, let what is obvious guide us to what is unknown, so that it may become clear what the blessed mourning is, which comfort follows. For if here it is the loss of goods we had that produces mourning, and no one would lament the loss of something unknown to him, then we must first know the good itself, what it truly is, and only then consider human nature. For in this way the blessed mourning will be attained. It is as with those who live in darkness. When one person is born in the gloom, while another, used to enjoying the light outside, is shut in through some mischance, the misfortune of their present state does not affect them both alike. The one, knowing what he has been deprived of, feels the loss of the light heavily; the other, never having known such a gift at all, lives without grief, since, having been reared in darkness, he reckons that he has lost none of the good things. As a result, desire to enjoy the light will drive the first to every device and scheme to see again what he was wrongfully deprived of, while the other will grow old living in the darkness, judging his present state to be good for himself because he does not know what is better. So too in the matter before us: whoever has been able to behold the truly good, and then

has considered the poverty of human nature, will surely have his soul in distress, and will mourn because the present life is not found in that good. So it seems to me that the Word does not call grief blessed, but the knowledge of the good, upon which the feeling of grief follows because what is sought is not present in this life. It follows, then, that we should examine what that light is which does not illumine this dark cave of human nature in the present life. Or perhaps desire is looking toward what is unattainable and incomprehensible? For what reasoning do we have that is able to track down the nature of what is sought? What meaning conveyed by nouns and verbs could produce in us a worthy notion of the light that lies beyond? How shall I name the invisible? How shall I represent the immaterial? How shall I show what has no form? How shall I grasp what has no size, no quantity, no quality, no shape; what is found neither in place nor in time; what lies beyond every limit and every defining image; whose work is life, and which is the very substance of all that is conceived as good; around which every lofty thought and name is contemplated: divinity, kingship, power, eternity, incorruption, joy and gladness, and everything that is conceived and spoken of on high? How, then, and by what reasonings, can such a good come within our view, that which beholds and is not seen? That which gives being to all that exists, while itself always is, and has no need of coming to be? But so that our discourse may not labor in vain, stretching itself out toward what cannot be contained, let us stop prying into the nature of the goods that lie beyond us, since it is impossible for such a thing to come within our comprehension. Let us take from our inquiry only this much gain: that through our very inability to see what is sought, we form some notion of the greatness of what we seek. And the higher by nature we believe the good to be than our knowledge, the more let us intensify our mourning, because the good from which we have been separated is of such a kind and so great that we cannot even contain the knowledge of it. Yet we human beings were once partakers of this good that surpasses every power of comprehension; and that good which is beyond all thought was so present in our nature that humanity seemed to be another such good, formed in the most exact likeness after the image of its prototype. For all that we now contemplate by conjecture concerning that good was also present in man: incorruption and blessedness, self-rule and freedom from any master, a life without grief and

without toil, a way of life among things more divine, and the power to look upon the good with a mind bare and clean of every veil. All this the account of the world's creation hints at for us in a few words, when it says that man was fashioned after the image of God, that he lived in paradise, and that he delighted in what was planted there. And the fruit of those plants was life and knowledge and the like. If, then, these things were once ours, how can anyone compare the present wretchedness with the blessedness of that time and not groan over the calamity? The lofty has been brought low; what was made in the image of the heavenly has become earthly; what was appointed to rule has been enslaved; what was created for immortality has been destroyed by death; what lived in the delights of paradise has been moved to this sickly and toilsome place; what was nurtured in freedom from passion has exchanged it for a life of passion and mortality; what was masterless and free to choose is now ruled by so many and such great evils that it is not even easy to count our tyrants. For each of the passions within us, when it gains the upper hand, becomes master of the one it has enslaved; and like a tyrant who has seized the citadel of the soul, it harms its subjects through those very subjects, using our own thoughts as servants for whatever it pleases. So it is with anger, with fear, cowardice, rashness, the passions of grief and of pleasure, hatred, strife, mercilessness, harshness, envy, flattery, resentment and callousness, and all the passions within us that are understood as opposed to the good: to list them is to list tyrants and masters, who enslave the soul to their own power like a captive taken in war. And if one should also reckon up the misfortunes of the body, which are entwined and bound up with our nature (I mean the varied and manifold forms of disease, of all of which humanity at first had no experience), the tears will flow far more abundantly, as one sees sorrows in place of goods side by side, and sets the evils against the better things. This, then, is what he who calls mourning blessed seems to teach in a hidden way: that the soul should look to the true good and not be submerged in the present deceit of life. For it is impossible for one who has examined things carefully to live without tears, and equally impossible for one sunk deep in the pleasures of life to think himself in sorrow. One can see this in the case of irrational animals. Their natural constitution is pitiable (for what is more pitiable than to lack reason?), yet they have no sense of their misfortune, but they too pass their lives in a kind of pleasure. The horse prances, the bull rolls in the dust, the boar bristles its mane, puppies play, calves frisk about, and every animal can be seen showing its pleasure by some sign; whereas if they had any understanding of the gift of reason, they would not spend their dumb and wretched lives in pleasure. So it is with human beings too: those who have no knowledge of the goods

of which our nature has been deprived pass their present life in pleasure. And taking pleasure in present things is followed by not seeking better things. But one who does not seek would not find what comes only to those who seek. That is why the Word calls mourning blessed: not judging it blessed in itself, but because of what comes from it. The way the saying is paired shows that mourning is blessed for them because of its relation to comfort. For "Blessed," he says, "are those who mourn"; and he did not end the sentence there, but added, "for they shall be comforted." It seems to me that the great Moses had foreseen this (or rather the Word who ordained these things through him in the mystical observances of the Passover), when he laid down for them unleavened bread on the feast days, and bitter herbs as a relish for the meal, so that through such riddles we might learn that there is no other way to share in that mystical feast unless the bitter herbs of this life are willingly mixed into a simple and unleavened life. For this reason the great David too, though he saw about himself the highest measure of human good fortune (I mean kingship), lavishly added bitter herbs to his own life, groaning in lamentation and bewailing the prolonging of his sojourn in the flesh, and fainting with longing for greater things. "Woe is me," he says, "that my sojourning is prolonged!" And elsewhere, gazing intently at the beauty of the divine dwellings, he says that he faints with longing, judging it better for himself to be placed among the lowest there than to hold first place among [?] the things of this present life. If anyone wishes to understand more precisely the force of this blessed mourning, let him consider for himself the story of Lazarus and the rich man, in which this teaching is made clear to us more plainly. "Remember," Abraham says to the rich man, "that you received your good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus in like manner evil things; therefore he is now comforted here, and you are in anguish." For it seems that our lack of counsel, or rather our evil counsel, drew us away from God's good ordering of human life. God had ordained for our enjoyment the good unmixed with evil, and had forbidden us to mix the experience of evil with what is noble; but we, out of gluttony, willingly gorged ourselves on its opposite (I mean that we tasted disobedience to the divine Word). For this reason human nature must certainly come to be in both states, and share in turn

both in what grieves and in what gladdens. Now there are two lives, and life is twofold, each of the two being considered in its own way; likewise gladness is twofold, one kind in this life, the other in the life laid up for us in hope. It would therefore be most blessed to store up our share of gladness, in true goods, for the eternal life, and to fulfil the service of grief in this short and passing life, counting it a loss not to be deprived of any of the pleasures of this life, but rather through enjoying them to fall away from better things. So if it is blessed to have a gladness without end, stretching on forever through the infinite ages, and human nature must in any case also taste the opposite, it is no longer hard to see the meaning of the saying, why those who mourn now are blessed: for they will be comforted for endless ages. And comfort comes from sharing in the Comforter. For the grace of comfort is the proper activity of the Spirit. May we too be counted worthy of it, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

"Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." Those with weak stomachs and poor appetites, say the experts in medicine, always feel full and sated because certain bad humors and residues have flowed together into the upper stomach. For this reason they turn away from wholesome food, since their natural appetite has withered under this false fullness. But if medical care is applied to them, and what is lodged in the hollows of the stomach is washed out by some purging draught, then, since the foreign matter no longer troubles their nature, their appetite for wholesome and nourishing food returns. And this, they say, is a sign of health: to take food no longer under compulsion, but with desire and eagerness. What, then, is the point of this preface? The Word leads us by the hand, advancing step by step to the higher rungs of the ladder of the Beatitudes; he is the one who, in the words of the Prophet, sets good ascents in our heart. After the ascents already completed, he now shows us another, a fourth, saying: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." Since this is so, I think it right that we should cleanse the soul, as far as possible, of its satiety and surfeit, and create in ourselves the blessed appetite for such food and drink.

For a person cannot be strong unless sufficient food supports his strength, nor can he be filled with food without eating, nor nourished without appetite. Since, then, strength is a good thing in life, and it is maintained by sufficient fullness, and fullness comes by eating, and eating comes from appetite, appetite would be a blessed thing for the living, since it is the beginning and cause of the strength that arises in us. But with this food that we perceive by the senses, not everyone desires the same things; the desire of those who partake is often divided among the kinds of food. One person delights in sweet things, another is drawn to what is pungent and heating, another enjoys salty foods, and another astringent ones. And it often happens that a person's craving for food does not arise according to what is good for him (for someone who, through some peculiarity of his temperament, is prone to a certain ailment feeds the disease with the quality of foods that work against him; whereas if he were drawn to what is beneficial, he would surely live in health, his food preserving his good condition). So too with the food of the soul: not everyone's desires incline toward the same thing. Some crave glory, or wealth, or some worldly distinction; the appetite of others is taken up with the table; still others eagerly take in envy as though it were some poisonous food; but there are some in whom what is good by nature becomes the object of appetite. And what is good by nature, always and for all, is that which is chosen not for the sake of something else, but is desirable for its own sake, always remaining the same and never dulled by satiety. For this reason the Word calls blessed not those who simply hunger, but those whose desire inclines toward true righteousness.

What, then, is righteousness? For I think this must first be uncovered by our discourse, so that once its beauty has been revealed, our appetite may be stirred toward the loveliness of what has appeared. For it is not possible to feel desire for what does not appear; our nature is somehow sluggish and unmoved toward the unknown, unless it gains some notion of what is desirable through hearing or sight. Now some of those who have examined such matters say that righteousness is a disposition that distributes what is equal, and to each what he deserves. For example, if someone is in charge of distributing money, he who looks to equality and proportions the gift to the need of the recipients is called just. And if someone who has received the authority to judge casts his vote not out of favor or enmity, but, following the nature of the facts, punishes those who deserve it, casts the vote that acquits for the innocent, and decides the other disputes according to the truth, he too is called just. So too the one who assigns taxes to his subjects, when he imposes a tax proportioned to their means; and the master of a household, and the ruler of a city,

and the king of nations: if each of these governs those under him fittingly, not moved by the irrational impulses that come from power, but judging his subjects with uprightness and adapting his mind to the wishes of those under his hand, then all such conduct is ascribed to the principle of righteousness by those who define the just as this kind of disposition. But I, looking to the aim of the divine legislation, conjecture that something more than what has been said is meant by this righteousness. For the saving word is common to all human nature, yet not every person holds the positions mentioned (for it belongs to few to be kings, rulers, judges, or to have control of money or some other administration, while the multitude are among the subjects and those who are administered). How, then, could anyone accept that true righteousness is something not set before all equally by nature? For if, according to the outside writers, the aim of the just is equality, and superiority involves inequality, it is impossible to think that the definition of righteousness they have given is true, since it is at once refuted by the inequality of life. What, then, is the righteousness that reaches to everyone? It is that righteousness the desire for which is set before all in common who look to the table of the Gospel, whether one is rich or poor, slave or master, nobly born or bought with money, since no circumstance either enlarges or diminishes the principle of the just. For if such a thing were found only in one who stands out through some authority and superiority, how was Lazarus just, cast down at the rich man's gate? He had no material for that kind of righteousness: no office, no authority, no house, no table, no other provision for life through which that righteousness could be practiced. For if being just consists in ruling, or distributing, or administering anything at all, then one who is not in those positions is altogether outside the just. How, then, is he counted worthy of rest who had none of the things by which, according to the common account, righteousness is characterized? So we must seek that righteousness whose enjoyment the one who desires it holds in promise. For "Blessed," he says, "are those who hunger for righteousness, for they shall be filled." Since many and various things are set before us to partake of, toward which human nature has the impulse of appetite, we have great need of knowledge so as to distinguish among such foods the nourishing from the poisonous, lest what the soul seems to take as food should work death and corruption in us instead of life. Perhaps it is not out of place to set out the meaning of this through another of the questions raised in the Gospel. He who shared with us in all things apart from sin

[?] and having shared the same sufferings with us, he did not judge hunger to be a sin, nor did he push away from his own experience the passion that goes with it. Instead he accepted nature's appetite, its impulse toward food. For after remaining without food for forty days, he was afterward hungry; when he wished, he gave nature the occasion to do its own work. But the inventor of temptations, when he learned that the passion of hunger had come upon him too, advised him to satisfy his appetite with stones. That is, he advised him to turn desire away from natural food toward things outside nature. "Command," he says, "that these stones become bread." What wrong has farming done? Why have seeds become so loathsome that the food that comes from them should be scorned? What fault is found with the Creator's wisdom, as though it did not rightly nourish humankind through seeds? For if stone now turns out to be more suitable for food, then God's wisdom has failed in the providence that human life requires. "Command that these stones become bread." He says this to this day to those who are tempted by their own appetite, and by saying it he usually persuades those who look to him to make their bread out of stones. For when appetite goes beyond the necessary limits of need, what else is this but the counsel of the devil? He then sets aside the food that comes from seeds and calls appetite out toward things beyond nature. Those people eat from stones who set before themselves the bread of greed, who prepare for themselves, out of injustice, tables worth many talents and swollen with luxury. The preparation of their banquets is a kind of display contrived to dazzle, and it strays outside what life needs. For what does the inedible substance of silver, set out in a weight so heavy it can hardly be lifted, have in common with nature's need? What is the passion of hunger? Is it not a longing for what is lacking? When our strength has been used up, what is lacking is made up again by a suitable addition. It is bread, or some other food, that nature longs for. If someone put gold to his mouth instead of bread, would that cure his want? So when someone seeks inedible materials before food, he is plainly busying himself with stones: nature seeks one thing while he is occupied with another. Through the passion of hunger nature all but cries aloud that it now needs food, because the body's spent strength has to be restored. But you do not listen to nature, for you do not give it what it asks. Instead you make sure that the load of silver on your table is great, you seek out smiths to work the metal, and you fuss over the scenes of figures engraved on it, so that art may render the passions and characters exactly in the carvings. One is meant to recognize the fury of the soldier as he raises his sword for the kill, and the agony of the wounded man who, doubled up from the mortal blow, seems by his posture to groan; the eagerness of the hunter and the ferocity of the beast; and whatever

else the vain lavish their artistry on, with such over-elaborate workmanship, in their tableware. Nature asked to drink, and you set out tripods worth many talents, basins and mixing bowls and jars, and countless other things that have nothing in common with the need in question. Through what you do, are you not plainly listening to the one who counsels you to look to stone? Why should anyone go through the rest of this stony food: the shameful spectacles and the entertainments that stir the passions? By these they pave for themselves the road to one evil after another, seasoning their food with the kindling of licentiousness. This is the adversary's counsel about food; this is what he suggests when he bids us look to stones instead of making the customary use of bread. But the destroyer of temptations does not banish hunger from nature as a cause of evils. He rejects only the excess that slips in alongside need at the adversary's prompting, and leaves nature to manage itself within its own bounds. Those who strain wine do not despise its usefulness because of the dregs mixed into it. They separate out what is superfluous with the strainer and do not throw away the use of what is pure. In the same way the Word, who discerns and separates out what is foreign to nature, did not banish hunger, with the fineness of his exact contemplation, since hunger preserves our life. But he strained out and threw away the excesses entangled with need, saying that he knows that bread to be nourishing which the word of God makes fit for nature. If, then, Jesus was hungry, hungering would be blessed when it is at work in us too in imitation of him. So if we learn what it is that the Lord hungers for, we shall surely learn the meaning of the beatitude now set before us. What, then, is the food that Jesus is not ashamed to desire? After his conversation with the Samaritan woman he says to the disciples: "My food is to do the will of my Father." And the will of the Father is plain, for he wants all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. If, then, he longs for us to be saved, and our life becomes his food, we have learned to what end we should use [?]

[?] the appetite, but now he has also made this good something to drink, so that by the passion of thirst he might show how hot and burning the desire is. For when we are thirsty we become, in a way, dry and fiery, and we take drink with pleasure as a remedy for that condition. Appetite for food and appetite for drink are one in kind, but our disposition toward each differs. So that the Word may lay down for us the highest degree of desire for the good, he blesses those who suffer both of these for righteousness, hunger and thirst alike. What is longed for can fit itself suitably to either appetite: it becomes solid food for the hungry, and drink for the one who draws in grace thirstily. "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." Is it blessed, then, to have an appetite for righteousness, while someone who feels the same way toward temperance, or wisdom, or prudence, or any other form of virtue is not called blessed by the Word? Perhaps what is said has rather some such meaning as this. Righteousness is one of the things that make up virtue. And divine Scripture, as is its custom, often embraces the whole by mentioning a part, as when it interprets the divine nature through certain names. For it says, "I am the Lord," the prophecy speaking as if in the person of God, "this is my everlasting name, and my memorial to all generations." And again elsewhere it says, "I am he who is." And in another place, "I am merciful." Holy Scripture knows how to name him by countless other names that signify what is lofty and befitting God. Through these we learn precisely that whenever it says one of them, the whole list of names is silently pronounced along with that one. For if he is called Lord, it is impossible that he should not also be the rest; all of them are named through one name. From this, then, we have learned that the inspired Word knows how to embrace many things through a part. So here too, when the Word says that righteousness is set before those who hunger in a blessed way, he signifies every form of virtue through it. The one who hungers for prudence, courage, temperance and whatever else is included in the same account of virtue is therefore equally blessed. For no single form of virtue, cut off from the rest, can by itself be perfect virtue. Whatever is not seen together with all that is understood as good necessarily leaves room for its opposite. Licentiousness is opposed to temperance and folly to prudence, and each of the things regarded as better certainly has something understood as its contrary. If, then, all of these were not seen together with righteousness, what was left could not possibly be good. For no one would call righteousness foolish, rash or licentious, or any-

thing else that is regarded as vicious. But if the account of righteousness is unmixed with anything worse, it has altogether embraced every good within itself; and the good is what is seen in virtue. Since all virtue is signified here by the name of righteousness, then, the Word blesses those who hunger and thirst, and promises that they will be filled with what they desire. "Blessed," he says, "are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." To me what is said seems to have some such meaning as this. None of the things pursued for pleasure in this life can satisfy those who pursue them. As Wisdom says somewhere in a riddle, preoccupation with pleasures is a leaking jar. Those who are eager for these things keep pouring into it diligently and show only an endless, fruitless labor. They are always pouring something into the depths of desire and heaping one pleasure on another, yet they never bring desire to the point of being filled. Who has ever found a limit to avarice in gaining what the avaricious strive for? Which glory-seeker ever stopped once he obtained what he was striving for? And the one who has glutted his pleasure with entertainments and spectacles, or with the frenzy and madness of the belly and what lies below the belly, what did he find left to him from such enjoyment? Does not every kind of pleasure fulfilled through the body fly away the moment it is reached, without staying with those who grasped it even for the briefest time? This lofty doctrine, then, we learn from the Lord: only the earnestness for virtue that arises in us is something firm and substantial. Someone who has achieved something lofty, such as temperance, or moderation, or piety toward the Divine, or any other of the lofty precepts of the gospel, does not take a passing and unstable joy in each of his achievements. His joy is settled and lasting, and it stretches over the whole span of his life. Why? Because these things can be practiced at all times, and no moment in the whole span of life brings on a surfeit of good activity. Temperance and purity, steadfastness in every good, and having no part in evil are always active as long as one looks to virtue, and the joy that comes with them stretches along with the activity. But with those who have poured themselves out in unseemly desires, even if their soul always looks toward licentiousness, enjoyment is not always at hand. Surfeit puts a stop to the madness for food, and the drinker's pleasure is quenched along with his thirst. The other pleasures in the same way need some time and interval, so that the appetite for what pleases, once it has withered from pleasure and fullness, may be roused again. But the possession of virtue, in those in whom it is firmly established, is neither measured by time nor limited by surfeit;

it always gives those who live by it a pure, fresh and flourishing sense of their own goods. Therefore the God Word promises to those who hunger for these things that they will be filled, but with a fullness that kindles appetite rather than dulling it. This, then, is what he teaches as he sets out the limits from the loftiness of his thoughts [?]. We are not to occupy our desire with anything of the kind where those who pursue it have no end in view, in which the pursuit is vain and foolish. Such people are like those who run after the head of their own shadow: their race leads nowhere, since what they chase always slips swiftly away ahead of the runner. Instead we are to turn our appetite toward things in which the pursuit becomes the pursuer's possession. For whoever desires virtue makes the good his own possession, seeing in himself what he desired. Blessed, then, is the one who has hungered for temperance, for he shall be filled with purity. And this fullness, as has been said, produces not aversion but a heightening of appetite, and the two grow together in equal measure. For the possession of what is desired follows on the desire for virtue, and the good that has taken root within brings unceasing joy with it into the soul. Such is the nature of this good that it does not only sweeten the life of the one who enjoys it in the present, but makes joy active in every part of time. The memory of a life rightly lived gladdens the one who achieved it. So does the present life, when it is led in virtue, and so does the expectation of reward. I take that reward to be nothing other than virtue itself, which is both the work of those who achieve it and their prize for what they have achieved. If I may venture on a bolder thought, it seems to me that perhaps, through this discourse on virtue and righteousness, the Lord is setting himself before the appetite of his hearers. He became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption; he is also the bread that comes down from heaven, and living water. David confesses in one of his psalms that he thirsted for him, offering this blessed passion of the soul to God when he says: "My soul has thirsted for God, the mighty, the living; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?" It seems to me that David, taught beforehand by the power of the Spirit these magnificent teachings of the Lord, also foretold that such an appetite would be satisfied for him. For he says, "I shall appear before your face in righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears to me." This, then, in my judgment, is true virtue: the good unmixed with anything worse, in which every thought

of things understood as better is included. It is God the Word himself, the virtue that has covered the heavens, as Habakkuk relates. Those who hunger for this righteousness of God are rightly called blessed. For truly, whoever has tasted the Lord, as the psalm says, that is, whoever has received God into himself, becomes full of what he thirsted and hungered for. So runs the promise of the one who said, "I and the Father will come and make our dwelling with him," the Holy Spirit clearly having made his dwelling there beforehand. So too, it seems to me, the great Paul, having tasted those ineffable fruits of paradise, was both full of what he had tasted and always hungry. He confesses that he has been filled with what he longed for when he says, "Christ lives in me"; and as one always hungry he strains forward to what lies ahead, saying, "Not that I have already obtained this or am already made perfect, but I run that I may lay hold of it." Let us be allowed to speak hypothetically of something that nature does not have. Suppose that in bodily eating nothing we take as food were excreted as waste, but the whole of it went into increasing our bodily height. Our bodies would then be raised to a great height, since each day's food would of itself add to their size. In the same way that righteousness, and all virtue along with it, is not excreted when it is eaten in the spiritual manner of eating. It therefore always makes those who share in it taller through itself, constantly increasing their stature by what it adds. If, then, we have understood the blessed hunger, let us vomit up all the surfeit that comes from vice and hunger for the righteousness of God, so that we may also come to be filled with it, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

"Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy." Perhaps it is something of this kind that Jacob was taught in a riddle through a vision, when he saw a ladder reaching from earth to the height of heaven, with God standing firmly upon it. The teaching of the beatitudes now does just this for us, always lifting those who climb by it to loftier thoughts. For there, I think, the life of virtue is portrayed for the patriarch in the form of a ladder. He was to learn for himself, and to teach those after him, that there is no other way to be lifted up to God than by always looking upward and keeping an unceasing desire for lofty things. One should not be content to remain with what has already been achieved, but should count it a loss not to lay hold of what lies beyond. Here too, then, through the beatitudes that follow one upon another, he prepares us to draw near to God himself, who is truly blessed and on whom all blessedness rests. Certainly, as we draw near to the

wise through wisdom and to the pure through purity, so we are made akin to the blessed one by way of the beatitudes. For blessedness truly belongs to God alone; that is why Jacob related that God stood firmly on such a ladder. Sharing in the beatitudes, then, is nothing other than communion with the Godhead, and it is to this that the Lord leads us up through what he says. It seems to me, then, that through the teaching of the beatitude set before us next he in a way makes the one who hears and understands his word divine. "Blessed," he says, "are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy." I know that in many places in divine Scripture the holy men call on the divine power by the name "merciful." David does so in his hymns, and Jonah in his prophecy, and the great Moses names the Divine in this way in many places of the Law. If, then, the title "merciful" befits God, what else is the word inviting you to become but God, formed, as it were, in the likeness of the Godhead? For if inspired Scripture calls God merciful, and the Godhead is what is truly blessed, the conclusion that follows is plain. Even if someone is a human being, when he becomes merciful he is counted worthy of divine blessedness, since he has come to be that by which the Divine is named. "The Lord is merciful and righteous, and our God shows mercy." How, then, could it not be a blessed thing for a human being to be called and to become that by which God is named from what he does? The divine Apostle, too, advises us in his own words to strive for the greater gifts. Our aim, however, is not to be persuaded to desire what is good, for that is naturally present in human nature, which leans of itself toward the good. Our aim is not to go wrong in judging what is good. It is above all in this respect that our life goes astray: we cannot discern precisely what is good by nature and what is only thought good through deception. For if vice were set before our life naked, and not colored with some appearance of good, humanity would not have deserted to it. We need understanding, then, to grasp the saying before us, so that once we have been taught the true beauty of the thought it contains, we may be formed according to it. The notion of the Divine is naturally present in all human beings, but ignorance of the God who truly is leads to differences over what is worshipped. Some revere the true Godhead, contemplated in Father, Son and Holy Spirit, while others have wandered into absurd notions, supposing that such a thing is to be found in creation; and so a small deviation from the truth opened the way to impiety. In just the same way, with the thought before us, if we do not grasp its true meaning, it is no small

…would be [?], and the loss would be ours if we were turned aside from the truth. What, then, is mercy, and on what is it exercised? And how is someone blessed by receiving back what he gives? For it says, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” The obvious meaning of the saying calls people to mutual love and compassion. Life is unequal and uneven, and not everyone lives in the same conditions, whether in rank, in bodily make-up or in any other kind of advantage. For the most part life is divided by opposites: it is split into slavery and mastery, wealth and poverty, glory and dishonour, bodily weakness and good health, and everything of that kind. So that what is lacking may be brought level with what has more, and what is deficient may be filled up from what is in excess, he lays down for humanity the law of mercy toward those who are worse off. For no one can set out to relieve a neighbour’s misfortune unless mercy has first softened the soul toward doing so. Mercy is understood from its opposite, harshness. Just as the harsh and savage man cannot be approached by those who come near him, so the compassionate and merciful man is somehow blended in feeling with the one in need, and becomes for the sufferer what the distressed mind longs for. If one were to put it in a definition, mercy is a voluntary grief that arises over the misfortunes of others. If we have not stated its meaning precisely, perhaps it can be explained more clearly in other words: mercy is a loving sharing of feeling with those who are distressed by painful things. For as harshness and brutality draw their impulse from hatred, so mercy somehow grows out of love, and could not arise from anything else. If anyone examines closely what is distinctive of mercy, he will find it to be an intensified loving disposition mingled with the feeling of grief. Everyone, enemies and friends alike, is eager to share in good things; but the wish to share in painful things belongs only to those who are ruled by love. And it is agreed that love is the best of all the things pursued in this life. Mercy is the intensification of love. Truly blessed, then, is the one whose soul has this disposition, since he reaches the very summit of virtue. And let no one see this virtue in material means alone. In that case it would be an achievement only for someone who has the means to do good. It seems to me fairer to look for it in the will.
