For whoever simply wills the good, but is prevented from doing what is right because he cannot, is in no way inferior in the disposition of his soul to the one who has shown his intention through deeds.

It would be superfluous to describe how much life gains if one takes the beatitude in this sense, since even small children can see what this counsel achieves in life. Suppose such an attitude toward the needy arose in everyone’s soul. Then there would no longer be superior and inferior. Life would no longer be divided between opposite names. Poverty would not distress anyone, slavery would not humble, dishonour would not grieve, for everything would be common to all. Equal rights and equal freedom of speech would govern human life, since the one who has more would voluntarily make himself equal to the one who lacks. And if this happened, no ground for enmity would remain. Envy would be idle, hatred dead, and resentment banished, along with lying, deceit and war, all of which are offspring of the desire for more. Once that unsympathetic disposition has been driven out, the shoots of vice are surely thrown out with it, as with an evil root. And when evils have been removed, the whole list of goods comes in to take their place: peace, justice, and the whole train of things we think of as better. What, then, could be more blessed than for life to be like this, when we no longer entrust the safety of our lives to bars and stones but are made safe in one another? Just as the harsh and brutish man makes enemies of those who have felt his savagery, so, conversely, we all become well-disposed toward the merciful, because mercy naturally engenders love in those who receive it. Mercy, then, as our discussion has shown, is the father of goodwill, the pledge of love, the bond of every friendly disposition. And what could anyone devise in life that is more secure than this security? So the Word rightly calls the merciful blessed, since so many good things are expressed by this name. But no one can fail to see that such counsel is useful for life. To me, however, the saying seems also to hint, in hidden terms, at something more than the obvious sense, concerning what we shall receive in the future. For it says, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy,” as though the recompense for mercy were stored up for the merciful later on. So let us leave this easily grasped meaning, which most people find readily, and as far as we are able let us attempt in our discourse to break through to what lies within the veil. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” There is something even loftier to learn from this saying, something touching doctrine. He who made man in his own image placed the beginnings of all good things in the nature of what he formed, so that nothing

good is brought into us from outside. Instead, it is in our power to be whatever we wish, bringing out the good from our nature as if from a storehouse. From the part we are taught about the whole: no one can obtain what he desires unless he grants the good to himself. That is why the Lord says somewhere to his hearers, “The kingdom of God is within you,” and, “Everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened.” So receiving what we long for, finding what we seek and coming within what we desire are in our power whenever we wish, and depend on our own choice. It follows that the opposite is also established: the inclination toward the worse comes about with no compulsion forcing it from outside. Evil comes into being at the very moment we choose it, when we choose it. In itself, as something with its own existence apart from choice, evil is found lying nowhere. From this the self-governing and free power that the Lord of nature built into human nature is clearly shown, since everything, whether good or worse, depends on our choice. And the divine judgment, following our purpose with an impartial and just verdict, assigns to each person what he happens to provide for himself. As the Apostle says, to those who by patience in good work seek glory and honour, it gives eternal life; but to those who disobey the truth and obey unrighteousness, it gives wrath and affliction and everything that goes by the names of grim [?]. Accurate mirrors show the faces in front of them just as those faces are: bright when people are cheerful, downcast when they are gloomy. No one would blame the mirror if the image looked gloomy because the original had fallen into dejection. In the same way the just judgment of God is shaped to our dispositions, and gives us back from our own store whatever we have given it. It says, “Come, you who are blessed,” and, “Depart, you who are cursed.” Is there some external compulsion here, allotting the sweet voice to those on the right and the grim one to those on the left? Did not the former obtain mercy through what they did, while the latter, by being harsh to their own kind, made the Divine harsh toward themselves? The rich man, sprawled in luxury, did not pity the poor man who suffered at his gate. For that reason he cut himself off from mercy, and he begged to be pitied and was not heard. This was not because one drop would have diminished the great spring of paradise, but because the drop of mercy cannot mix with harshness. For what fellowship has light with darkness? It says, “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For whoever sows to his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but whoever sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap life

eternal.” I take the sowing to be human choice, and the harvest to be the recompense for that choice. Rich is the ear of good things for those who have chosen such sowing; laborious is the gathering of thorns for those who cast thorny seed into their lives. For a person must reap whatever he has sowed; it cannot be otherwise. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” What human speech could fathom the depth of the thoughts contained in this saying? The absolute and unqualified form of the expression allows us to explore something more than what has already been said, because it does not add who those are toward whom mercy should be active, but simply says, “Blessed are the merciful.” Perhaps the saying hints at something like this: that the meaning of mercy follows on from blessed mourning. There, too, the one who spends this life in mourning was called blessed, and here the saying seems to me to suggest the same teaching. Consider how we feel about other people’s misfortunes, when some of our friends meet with unwelcome sorrows. Perhaps they have been driven from their father’s house, or saved naked from a shipwreck, or have fallen into the hands of pirates or brigands. Perhaps they have become slaves after being free, or captives after being prosperous, or have met some other such evil, though until then they had been counted among the fortunate. In such cases our souls feel a painful sympathy. It would surely be far more fitting to feel this way about ourselves, because of the undeserved change in our life. For when we consider what a splendid house we were driven from; how we fell into the hands of brigands; how we were sunk in the deep of this life and stripped naked; how many masters, and what masters, we have brought upon ourselves in place of freedom and a self-governed life; how we cut short the blessedness of life with death and corruption — when we take these thoughts to heart, is it possible to spend our pity on the misfortunes of others, and not have the soul pity itself as it reckons what it had and what it has lost? What is more pitiable than this captivity? Instead of the delights of paradise, our lot in life is this sickly and toilsome place. Instead of that freedom from passion, we have received in exchange the countless deadly blows of the passions. Instead of that lofty way of life, the life shared with the angels, we have been condemned to live with the beasts of the earth, having exchanged the angelic and passionless life for the life of cattle. And who could easily count the bitter tyrants of our life, the raging and savage masters? Anger is a bitter master. Envy is another of the same kind. Hatred, and the passion of pride, are raging and

savage tyrants. Licentious thought is like a master who abuses slaves bought with silver, for it enslaves our nature to passionate and impure services. And what extreme of bitterness does the tyranny of greed not exceed? Once it has enslaved the wretched soul, it forces it always to satisfy its insatiable desires. It is always receiving and never filled, like a many-headed beast passing food through countless mouths into an unfillable belly. There is never any limit to gain. Whatever is taken becomes fuel and kindling for the desire for more. Who, then, could consider this miserable life and remain pitiless and harsh toward such misfortunes? The reason we do not pity ourselves is that we are insensible of our ills. It is like what happens to people deranged by madness: the very extremity of their illness has also taken away any awareness of what they are suffering. So suppose someone came to know himself, what he once was and what he is now. As Solomon says somewhere, “Those who know themselves are wise.” Such a person will never stop feeling pity, and divine mercy will naturally follow on such a disposition of soul. That is why it says, “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” They themselves, and not others. In this it makes the word clear, as if someone were to say, “It is a blessed thing to look after one’s bodily health,” because the one who looks after it will himself live in health. In the same way the merciful man is blessed, because the fruit of mercy becomes the merciful man’s own possession. This holds whether we take the meaning we have just found or the one examined earlier, which I mean shows the soul’s compassion for the misfortunes of others. Each is equally good: to pity oneself in the way described, and to suffer with one’s neighbours in their misfortunes. For the justice of the divine judgment applies to a person, from the higher authority, the same choice he made toward those beneath him. In a way, then, a person is his own judge, casting the vote on himself as he judges those under him. It is believed, and truly believed, that all human nature will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done in the body, whether good or bad. Perhaps it is even bold to say this, but if it is possible to grasp by reasoning things that are unspeakable and unseen, we may already perceive the blessedness of the recompense of those who have obtained mercy. The goodwill that arises in souls toward those who show them mercy will probably remain forever, beyond this life, in the life to come, among those who have received the favour. What, then, is likely to happen at the time of the examination? If the benefactor is recognized by those he has helped, how will his soul feel as he is praised with thankful voices before God and all creation?

Will he need any further blessing, when he is proclaimed for his excellence in so great a theatre? The voice of the Gospel teaches that those who have been helped will be present, in the King’s judgment of the righteous and of the sinners. To both he uses the demonstrative, as though pointing out with his finger who is standing there: “Inasmuch as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers.” By saying “these” he shows that those who were helped are present. Now let the one who values the lifeless stuff of money above the blessedness to come tell me: what brilliance of gold can compare with this? What gleam of precious stones? What adornment of clothing is like the good that hope sets before us? The King of creation will reveal himself to human nature, seated in majesty on his lofty throne. The countless myriads of angels will be seen around him. The ineffable kingdom of heaven will come before the eyes of all, and opposite it the fearful places of punishment will be displayed. In the midst of these all human nature, everyone born from the first creation to the consummation of all things, will stand in suspense, between fear and hope of what is to come, often shaken as it awaits one outcome or the other. Even those who have lived with a good conscience will be unsure of the future when they see others dragged down by their evil conscience into that grim darkness, as if by an executioner. If, at that moment, this man is brought before the judge by his works, amid the praising and thankful voices of those he has helped, and shining with confidence, will he think that good fortune is anything like material wealth? Would he accept, in exchange for those goods, every mountain and plain and glen and the sea turned into gold for him? But think of the one who carefully hid his mammon away with seals and bars, iron-bound gates and secure hiding places, and judged that the stuff buried away in secret for himself was worth more than every commandment. He will be dragged headlong to the dark fire, while all who experienced him in this life throw his harshness and savagery in his face, saying: “Remember that you received your good things in your lifetime. You locked mercy away together with your wealth in its strongholds, and left compassion behind on earth. You did not bring kindness with you to this life here. You do not have what you did not hold; you do not find what you did not store up; you do not gather what you did not scatter; you will not reap what you did not sow. The harvest matches your sowing. You sowed bitterness: gather the sheaves. You prized mercilessness: have what you loved. You did not look on others with compassion: you will not be looked on with pity. You overlooked the afflicted: you will be overlooked

as you perish. You fled from mercy: mercy will flee from you. You loathed the poor: he who became poor for your sake will loathe you.” If these and similar things are said, where is the gold? Where are the splendid vessels? Where is the security of the seals placed on the treasures? Where are the dogs posted for the night watches, and the store of weapons against plotters? Where is the inventory written down in the books? What use are these against the weeping and the gnashing of teeth? Who will light up the darkness? Who will quench the flame? Who will turn away the undying worm? Let us, then, understand the Lord’s voice, brothers, which teaches us so much about the future in so few words. And let us become merciful, so that by this we may become blessed, in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory and power to the ages of ages. Amen.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Picture people looking down from a high mountain ridge into a vast, open sea. My mind has felt what they are likely to feel, as from this lofty saying of the Lord, as if from a mountain peak, it gazes into the bottomless depth of its meaning. In many places along the coast one can see a mountain cut in half, sheared straight down on the seaward side from summit to base, with a headland at its top jutting out and leaning over the deep. A person who peers down from such a lookout, from that great height, to the sea far below, is likely to feel dizzy. In the same way my soul now grows dizzy, suspended aloft by this great saying of the Lord: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” God is promised as the sight for those whose hearts have been purified. Yet “No one has ever seen God,” as the great John says. And Paul, lofty in thought, confirms it, saying, “whom no one has seen or can see.” This is the smooth and sheer rock that offers our thoughts no footing on itself. Moses likewise declared it inaccessible in his teaching, so that our mind can nowhere get a foothold, for his denial has shaved away every handhold. “For there is no one,” he says, “who shall see the Lord and live.” Yet to see God is eternal life. And the pillars of the faith, John and Paul and Moses, declare this to be impossible. Do you see the dizziness with which the soul is drawn toward the depth of what this saying contemplates? If God is life, then whoever does not see him does not see life. And the God-inspired among the prophets and apostles testify that it is impossible to see God. To what, then, is human hope reduced? But the Lord holds up hope as it falls.

It is like what he did for Peter, who was in danger of sinking: he set him again on water that had become solid and firm beneath him. If, then, the hand of the Word should reach us too, and set us, unsteady as we are in the depths of these speculations, upon firm thought, we shall be free of fear, holding fast to the Word who leads us by the hand. For "Blessed," he says, "are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." The promise is so great that it passes beyond the furthest limit of blessedness. For after such a good, what else could anyone desire, since he has everything in the One he has seen? In the usage of Scripture, "to see" means the same as "to have." So in "May you see the good things of Jerusalem," the phrase means "May you find"; and in "Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord," the prophet means by "not see" that he will "not share in" it. So whoever has seen God has, by that seeing, come to possess everything that is counted among good things: endless life, everlasting incorruption, deathless blessedness, the unending kingdom, unceasing gladness, the true light, the spiritual and sweet voice, the unapproachable glory, perpetual exultation, every good. This is what the promise of the beatitude sets before our hope, and this is how great it is. But since it has been shown that the way to see is to become pure in heart, my mind again grows dizzy at this point. Perhaps purity of heart is one of those things that are impossible and beyond our nature. For if this is how God is seen, yet Moses and Paul did not see him, and declared that neither they nor anyone else could see him, then what the Word now sets before us in the beatitude seems to be impossible. What do we gain, then, by knowing how God is seen, if our mind has no power to do it? It would be as if someone said that it is blessed to be in heaven, because there one will see what is not seen in this life. If the saying had also shown some means of travelling to heaven, then it would be useful for the hearers to learn that being there is most blessed. But as long as the ascent is impossible, what good does knowing about heavenly blessedness do? It only grieves those who have learned of it, by showing them what they are deprived of because they cannot ascend. Does the Lord, then, command what lies beyond our nature, and has the greatness of his command exceeded the limits of human power? That is not so. He does not command creatures to fly when he has not given them wings, or to live under water when he has assigned them a life on land. In everything else, then, the law suits the capacity of those who receive it and forces nothing beyond their nature. So it follows that we should understand this case the same way: what the beatitude holds out to us is not beyond hope. And we should understand also that

John, Paul, Moses and anyone else like them have not fallen short of this lofty blessedness that comes from seeing God. This is true of the one who said, "There is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the righteous judge will give me"; of the one who leaned on Jesus' breast; and of the one who heard the divine voice say, "I know you above all." Those who proclaimed that knowing God is beyond our power are without doubt blessed. But blessedness consists in seeing God, and this comes from becoming pure in heart. Therefore purity of heart, through which one can become blessed, is not impossible. How, then, can we say that those who, with Paul, declare the knowledge of God to be beyond our power are speaking the truth, and also that the Lord's voice does not contradict them when it promises that God will be seen by those who are pure? [?]

It seems to me right first to deal with this briefly, so that our study of the subject may proceed in order. Whatever the divine nature is in itself, in its essence, it lies beyond every thought that tries to grasp it. Our guesses and reasonings cannot reach it or come near it. No one has yet found a human faculty that can understand the incomprehensible, and no method has been devised for grasping what is beyond our powers. This is why the great Apostle calls his ways "unsearchable." By this word he means that reasoning cannot travel the road that leads to knowledge of the divine essence. It is as though none of those who went before us in life had left any trace of understanding to mark the way toward knowledge of what lies beyond knowledge. Yet although he who is above every nature is such by nature, he who is invisible and uncircumscribed is seen and grasped in another way. There are many ways of perceiving him like this. For it is possible, through the wisdom that appears in the universe, to see by inference him who made all things in wisdom. In the same way, with human works, the mind in some sense sees the maker of the object in front of it, because he has put his skill into the work. Yet what is seen is not the craftsman's nature, but only the craftsmanship that he has put into what he made. So too, when we look at the order of creation, we form an idea not of the essence but of the wisdom of him who made all things wisely. And when we consider the cause of our own life, and see that he came to create man not from necessity but from a good choice, we say that in this way too we have seen God, because we have come to know his goodness, though not his essence. So too with everything else that lifts our

thought toward what is better and higher: we call such things knowledge of God, since each of these lofty thoughts brings God into our view. For power, purity, unchangeableness, freedom from any mixture with its opposite, and all such things impress on our souls the image of a divine and lofty conception. What has been said, then, shows how the Lord speaks the truth when he promises that those with a pure heart will see God, and also how Paul does not lie when he declares in his own words that no one has seen God or can see him. For he who is invisible by nature becomes visible in his activities, and he is seen in certain things that surround him. But the meaning of the beatitude is not limited to this, that from some activity one can infer what the one acting is like. Perhaps even the wise of this age might come to know the transcendent wisdom and power through the harmony of the world. Rather, the greatness of the beatitude seems to me to suggest another piece of advice to those who are able to receive it, about how to see what they long for. I will explain the thought that has occurred to me with examples. Bodily health is one of the good things in human life. But the blessing is not merely to know what health is; it is to live in health. If someone recited the praises of health, yet chose food that was unwholesome and full of bad humours, what good would those praises do him while illness wore him down? Let us understand the present saying in the same way. The Lord does not say that it is blessed to know something about God, but to have God within oneself. For "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." It does not seem to me that he presents God as a sight placed in front of the one whose soul's eye has been cleansed. Rather, perhaps the greatness of the saying suggests to us what the Word states more plainly to others when he says, "The kingdom of God is within you." This teaches us that whoever has cleansed his own heart of every created thing and every passionate disposition sees the image of the divine nature in his own beauty. And it seems to me that in these few words the Word gives some such advice as this: "O men, all of you who have any desire to contemplate the true good, when you hear that the divine majesty is exalted above the heavens, that its glory cannot be expressed, its beauty cannot be described, and its nature cannot be contained, do not fall into despair of ever seeing what you long for. For what you are able to contain, the

measure of the knowledge of God, is within you, since he who formed you built this good into your nature from the very beginning. For God imprinted on your makeup copies of the good things of his own nature, as one presses the shape of an engraving into wax. But wickedness, poured over that God-like stamp, has made the good useless to you, hidden as it is under shameful coverings. If, then, by living carefully you wash off again the filth that has caked onto your heart, the God-like beauty will shine out in you once more." This is what naturally happens with iron. When a whetstone has stripped off its rust, the iron that was black a moment before glints in the sun and gives off rays and flashes of light. So too the inner man, whom the Lord calls the heart, when he has scraped off the rusty filth that evil mould has caused to bloom over his form, will recover his likeness to the archetype and will be good. For what is like the good is certainly good. So whoever looks at himself sees within himself what he longs for. This is how the pure in heart become blessed: looking at their own purity, they see the archetype in the image. People who see the sun in a mirror, even without gazing directly at the sky, see the sun in the mirror's brightness no less than those who look at the sun's disc itself. "So too," he says, "even if you are too weak to look upon the light, you have what you seek within yourselves, if you return to the grace of the image that was built into you from the beginning. For the Godhead is purity, freedom from passion, and separation from every evil. If these things are in you, then God is certainly in you. So when the mind within you is unmixed with any wickedness, free from passion and separated from every defilement, you are blessed for the sharpness of your sight. Having been cleansed, you have perceived what those who are not cleansed cannot see. The mist of material things has been removed from the eyes of your soul, and you see the blessed sight clearly in the clear, bright sky of your heart." And what is this sight? Purity, holiness, simplicity, and all such shining rays of the divine nature, through which God is seen. From what has been said, we do not doubt that these things are so. Yet our argument still faces the same difficulty that was raised at the beginning. Whoever comes to be in heaven shares in the wonders of heaven, but there is no way to ascend, and so none of what we have agreed on does us any good. In the same way, no one doubts that blessedness comes from cleansing the heart, but how anyone might cleanse it of its defilements seems just as hard as climbing up to heaven. What ladder of Jacob, then, or what fiery chariot like the one that carried the prophet Elijah up to heaven, can be found to lift our heart to the wonders above,

so that it may shake off this earthly weight? If someone considers the passions of the soul that we cannot escape, he will think it hopeless and impossible to get away from the evils bound up with us. From the very start our birth begins in passion, our growth proceeds through passion, and our life ends in passion. Evil has somehow been mixed into our nature through those who first accepted passion, who brought the disease to live in us by their disobedience. The nature of animals continues through the succession of offspring of each kind, so that what is born has the same nature as what it was born from. In the same way, man is born from man, the passionate from the passionate, the sinner from the sinner. So sin in a way comes into existence along with those who are born. It is born with them and grows up with them, and it ends with them at the end of their life. Moreover, we have been taught in many places in divine Scripture that virtue is hard for us to attain, and that it is achieved only with difficulty, through countless sweats and toils, through effort and labour. We have heard that the way of the kingdom is hard and runs through a narrow path, while the way that leads life through wickedness to destruction is broad, downhill and easy to run along. Yet Scripture has not declared the lofty life altogether impossible, since in its holy books it has recorded the wonderful deeds of so many men. But the promise of seeing God has a twofold meaning. One is to know the nature that is above all things; the other is to be united with him through purity of life. The voice of the saints declares that the first kind of knowledge is impossible. The second the Lord promises to human nature through the present teaching when he says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God." How one can become pure you can learn from nearly the whole of the gospel teaching. If you run through the commandments that follow, you will clearly find how the heart is cleansed. He divides wickedness into two kinds: that which is done in deeds, and that which takes shape in thoughts. Formerly, through the ancient law, he punished the injustice that shows itself in deeds. Now he has made the law look to the other kind of sin. He does not punish the evil deed, but takes care that it should not even begin. For removing wickedness from the will is a far more effective way of making a life free of evil deeds. And since wickedness has many parts and many forms, he has set against each forbidden thing its own remedy in the commandments. Anger is an ailment that is ready to hand in almost every part of life, so he begins his cure with what is most prevalent and makes freedom from anger his first law. "You have been taught by the older

law," he says, "'You shall not murder.' Now learn to remove from your soul anger against your own kind." He did not forbid anger altogether, since this impulse of the soul can sometimes be used for good. What the commandment put out was being angry with one's brother for no good reason. For he says, "Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause." The addition of "without cause" shows that using anger is often fitting, when the passion boils up to punish sin. The word of Scripture had already borne witness to this kind of anger in Phinehas, when by killing the lawbreakers he turned aside God's threat that had been stirred up against the people. Next he moves on with his cure to the sins committed through pleasure, and by his commandment he removes from the heart the wicked desire for adultery. In the same way you will find the Lord in what follows correcting each sin one by one, setting his laws against each form of wickedness. He prevents unjust violence from starting by not even allowing retaliation. He drives out the passion of greed by commanding us to strip off even what is left and give it to the one who has robbed us. He cures cowardice by commanding us to despise death. In short, in each of the commandments you will find the word working like a plough, digging up from the depths of our heart the evil roots of sins, so that we may be cleansed of their thorny crop. So he does good to our nature in two ways: by promising the good, and by giving us the teaching that leads to what he has set before us. If striving for what is good seems laborious to you, compare it with the opposite life. You will find how much more laborious wickedness is, if not in the present, then when you look to what comes after. For whoever has heard of Gehenna will no longer need toil or effort to separate himself from the pleasures of sin. Fear alone, once it enters his thoughts, will be enough to drive out the passions. Or rather, it is good to notice what is implied though not said, and to take from it a stronger desire. If the pure in heart are blessed, then those whose minds are defiled are certainly pitiable, because they look upon the face of the adversary. And if the divine stamp itself is imprinted on the life of virtue, then clearly the life of wickedness becomes the form and face of the adversary. Indeed, if God is named, according to different ways of conceiving him, by each of the things understood as good, such as light, life, incorruption and everything of that kind, then by the same reasoning in reverse, the inventor of wickedness will be named by the opposite of each of these: darkness, death, corruption and everything akin and related to them. We have learned, then, what shapes wickedness and what shapes the life of virtue, and by the free choice of our will we have the power to take either one. So let us flee the form of the devil, take off the evil mask, take up again the divine image, and become pure in

"Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God." In the holy tabernacle of witness, which the lawgiver built for the Israelites after the pattern God showed him on the mountain, everything enclosed within the boundary was holy and sacred. But the innermost part was an inaccessible sanctuary that no one could enter, called the Holy of Holies. I think this intensive form of the name shows that it did not share in holiness on equal terms with the other things. Rather, it shows that this sanctuary was as much holier and purer than the holy things around it as what is consecrated and holy is different from what is common and profane. In the same way, I think, all the beatitudes shown to us on this mountain, which the divine Word set up one by one before this, are sacred and holy, but the one now set before us for contemplation is truly an inner sanctuary and Holy of Holies. If seeing God is a good that nothing can surpass, then becoming a son of God is surely beyond every good fortune. What words could be devised, what meaning could names carry, that would capture the gift of so great a promise? Whatever anyone conceives in his mind, what is meant here is certainly beyond it. If you call what this beatitude promises good, precious or lofty, what is meant is more than these names can express. Its attainment is beyond what we could pray for, the gift is beyond hope, the grace is beyond nature. What is man, compared with the divine nature? Which of the saints shall I quote to show how lowly human beings are? According to Abraham, man is earth and ashes; according to Isaiah, grass; according to David, not even grass, but like grass. For Isaiah says, "All flesh is grass," while David says, "Man is like grass." According to Ecclesiastes, man is vanity; according to Paul, wretchedness. The words the Apostle used for himself express pity for all humanity. This is what man is. But God, who is he? How shall I say what he is, when he cannot be seen, or contained by the hearing, or grasped by the heart? With what words shall I proclaim his nature? What example of this good shall I find among the things we know? What new words shall I invent to express what cannot be spoken or uttered? I have heard the divinely inspired Scripture tell of great things about the transcendent nature. But what are these, compared with that nature itself? For the word said as much as I was able to receive, not as much as the

…what is signified. Think of people breathing the air. Each takes in as much as his own capacity allows, one more and another less. Yet the one who holds a great deal of air within himself has not taken the whole element inside him. He too has taken from the whole only as much as he could, and the whole remains entire. In the same way, the teachings about God in holy Scripture, set out for us by those whom the Holy Spirit moved, are lofty and great by the measure of our understanding, beyond all greatness. Yet they do not reach the true greatness. "Who has measured the heavens with a span," it says, "and the water with his hand, and all the earth with a handful?" Do you see how grandly he describes the inexpressible power? But what are these things compared with that which truly is? In such grand words the text has taken in only a part of the divine activity. As for the power from which the activity comes, to say nothing of the nature from which the power comes, it neither spoke of it nor tried to. It even rebukes those who portray the Divine by guesswork, saying as if in the person of God, "To whom have you likened me? says the Lord." Ecclesiastes lays down the same counsel in his own words: "Do not be hasty to utter a word before the face of God, for God is in heaven above, and you are on earth below." By the distance between the elements he shows, I think, how far the divine nature rises above earthly reasonings. Yet to this reality, so great and of such a kind, which can be neither seen nor heard nor reasoned out, man is made kin. Man, counted as nothing among the things that exist, dust, grass, vanity, is adopted by the God of the universe into the rank of a son. What thanks could be found worthy of this grace? What voice, what thought, what movement of the mind could praise its surpassing greatness? Man goes beyond his own nature: mortal, he becomes immortal; perishable, incorruptible; short-lived, eternal; in short, from man he becomes god. For whoever has been counted worthy to become a son of God will surely have in himself the dignity of the Father, and becomes heir of all the Father's goods. O the generosity of the rich Master! O the open palm! O the great hand! How great are the gifts from the treasures beyond words! Out of his love for humanity he raises the nature that sin had dishonored almost to equal honor with himself. For if he grants human beings kinship with what he himself is by nature, what else is he promising than a kind of equal honor through that kinship?

Such, then, is the prize. What is the contest? "If you make peace," he says, "you will be crowned with the grace of adoption." To me it seems that the very work for which he promises so great a reward is itself another gift. For what is sweeter to human beings, for enjoying the things they pursue in life, than a peaceful life? Name any of life's pleasures you like: it needs peace in order to be pleasant. Suppose you had everything that is prized in life: wealth, good health, a wife, children, a house, parents, servants, friends, land and sea each enriching you with its own goods; parks, hunting, baths, wrestling grounds, gymnasia, places of luxury and youthful amusement, and every invention of pleasure. Add to these pleasant spectacles and music to listen to, and anything else that sweetens life for those who live in luxury. If you had all these, but the good of peace were absent, what would you gain from them, when war cuts off the enjoyment of your goods? So peace is pleasant in itself to those who share in it, and it also sweetens everything that is prized in life. Even if we suffer some misfortune in time of peace, as humans do, the evil is mixed with good and becomes easier for those who suffer it. But when war grips our life, we become in a way numb to such occasions of grief, for the common calamity outweighs the private ones in pain. Physicians say of bodily ailments that if two pains strike one body at the same time, only the stronger is felt. The pain of the lesser evil somehow goes unnoticed, stolen away by the onset of the one that prevails. In the same way the evils of war, which surpass all others in pain, make each person insensible to his own misfortunes. And if the soul is somehow numbed to its own evils, stunned by the common evils of war, how will it be able to feel any pleasure? Where there are weapons and horses and sharpened iron and blaring trumpets; phalanxes bristling with spears, shields locked together, helmets nodding fearfully with their crests; clashes, shoving, grappling, battles, slaughter, flights, pursuits, wailing, war cries, earth soaked with blood, the dead trampled underfoot, the wounded left behind, and all the other bitter things that war brings, will anyone caught up in these ever be able to turn his mind to the memory of something that gladdens? And if a memory of something most delightful should steal into the soul, does not the recollection of what is dearest, coming to mind in a time of danger, only add to the calamity? So he who rewards you for keeping clear of the evils of war has given you two gifts. One gift is the prize; the other gift is the contest itself. Even if nothing were promised to it in hope, peace for its own sake would be preferred to every pursuit by anyone with sense. Here, then, we can recognize the surpassing greatness of his love for humanity: he has granted good rewards not for toil and sweat, but, in a way, for enjoyment and delight, if indeed

peace is the chief of all that gladdens us. He wants it to be present to each person in such measure that each not only has it himself but, out of great abundance, shares it with those who lack it. For he says, "Blessed are the peacemakers." A peacemaker is one who gives peace to another, and no one can give another what he does not have himself. So he wants you first to be full of the good things of peace, and then to hold them out to those who are in need of such a possession. Let us not labor too much over the deeper contemplation, for the plain meaning is enough to help us gain what is good. "Blessed are the peacemakers." In a few words the saying offers a cure for many illnesses: with this summary and more general expression it takes in all the particulars. Let us first consider what peace is. What else than a loving disposition toward those of our own kind? What, then, is understood as the opposite of love? Hatred, anger, wrath, envy, resentment, hypocrisy, the calamity of war. Do you see how many illnesses, and of what kind, this one word is an antidote for? Peace stands against each of the things just named alike, and by its presence makes the evil vanish. Just as disease disappears when health takes hold, and no darkness remains when light appears, so when peace appears, all the passions that arise from its opposite are dissolved. How great a good this is I need not describe myself; you have worked it out for yourself. Consider what life is like for people who regard one another with suspicion and hatred. Meeting each other is hateful to them, and everything about the other is loathsome. Their mouths are silent, their glances turned away, their ears stopped against the voice of the one who hates and is hated. Whatever is dear to one is whatever is not dear to the other; and, conversely, whatever pleases his enemy he counts hostile and hateful. Fragrant spices fill the air around them with their own sweet scent. In the same way he wants the grace of peace to overflow in you so abundantly that your life becomes a cure for the sickness of others. You would recognize more exactly how great such a good is if you reckoned up the calamities brought by each of the passions that arise in the soul from a hostile disposition. Who could describe the sufferings of anger as they deserve? What words could sketch the ugliness of this disease? You see the symptoms of the demon-possessed appearing in those who are overcome by wrath. Compare the symptoms of the demon and of wrath side by side, and see what difference there is between them. The eye of the possessed is bloodshot and rolling, the tongue raving, the speech harsh, the voice shrill and barking. These are common to wrath and to the demon alike: the shaking head, the frantic movements of the hands, the convulsing of the whole body,

the unsteady feet. The same signs describe both diseases. They differ from each other only in this: the one is a voluntary evil, while the other falls on its victims against their will. And how much more pitiable is it to fall into calamity by one's own impulse than to suffer it against one's will! Whoever sees the disease caused by a demon certainly pities it. But the frenzy caused by anger he sees and imitates at the same moment, thinking it a loss if he does not outdo, in his own passion, the one who fell sick first. Moreover, the demon wrenches the body of its victim but stops the evil there, flinging the madman's hands at random through the air. The demon of wrath, however, does not leave the body's movements without effect. When the passion prevails and the blood around the heart boils over, black bile, as they say, is scattered through the whole body by the wrathful disposition. Then, under the vapors pressing from within, all the sense organs of the head are cramped. The eyes are forced out beyond the rims of the eyelids and glare, bloodshot and snakelike, at whatever is vexing them. The inner parts are seized by panting. The veins along the neck swell, the tongue thickens, and as the windpipe narrows the voice becomes shrill [?]. Through the spread of that cold bile the lips congeal and turn dark, and they become hard to open and close as they naturally should, so that the man cannot even hold back the spittle collecting in his mouth. He spits it out along with his words, his strained voice spraying foam. Then you can also see the hands set in motion by the disease, and the feet likewise. And these limbs no longer move in vain, as happens with the possessed, but to the harm of those whom the disease sets grappling with one another. For at once those striking one another aim their blows at the vital organs of sense. And if somewhere in the struggle a mouth comes near a body, not even the teeth stay idle; like a wild beast's they fasten on whatever they come close to. Who could list one by one all the evils that have their origin in anger? So whoever prevents such ugliness would rightly be called blessed and honored for the greatest of benefits. If someone who frees a person from some bodily affliction is honored for that good deed, how much more will someone who frees the soul from this disease be regarded by those with sense as a benefactor of life itself! For as much as the soul is better than the body, so much more honorable than those who heal bodies is the one who heals souls. And let no one suppose that, among the evils that hatred produces, I think the ugliness of anger is the worst. To me the passion of envy and hypocrisy seems much worse than the one

just mentioned, since what is hidden is more dangerous than what is in plain view. With dogs, too, we are more on our guard against those whose anger is announced neither by a bark nor by a frontal attack, but which, with a gentle and tame manner, lie in wait for a moment when we are off guard and unsuspecting. Such is the passion of envy and hypocrisy. Hatred is nursed secretly within, in the depths of the heart, like a fire, while hypocrisy shapes the outward appearance into friendship. Suppose a fire is hidden under chaff. For a while it smolders within, burning what lies next to it, but no flame shows outside. Only a pungent smoke, forcibly pressed from within, finds its way out; and if it catches a draught, it is fanned into a bright and visible flame. So envy, too, eats away the heart from within, as fire eats a tightly packed heap of chaff. Out of shame it hides the disease, yet it cannot hide it completely. Like pungent smoke, the bitterness of envy shows through in the symptoms of a person's appearance. And if some misfortune touches the one who is envied, then the envious man reveals his disease, turning the other's grief into his own gladness and pleasure. While the passion thinks it escapes notice, its hidden workings are betrayed by plain signs on the face. The signs seen in those whose lives are despaired of often appear in one who is wasted by envy: dry eyes sunk beneath hardened lids, a drooping brow, bones showing through the flesh. And what is the cause of the disease? That a brother, or a relative, or a neighbor lives in good cheer [?]. O strange new kind of injury! To make it a grievance that the other is not unfortunate, and to be pained at his success! He judges that he has been wronged not by any harm he has suffered at the other's hands, but because the other, who has done no wrong, has what he desires. What has happened to you, wretched man? So I would say to him. Why are you wasting away, eyeing your neighbor's prosperity with a bitter eye? What charge can you bring? That he is handsome? That he is eloquent? That he is of better birth? That he has risen to some office and is seen shining in his rank? That he has come into some wealth? That his good sense commands respect when he speaks? That many admire him for his benefactions? That he takes pride in his children? That he delights in his wife? That the revenues of his house make him splendid? Why do these things strike your heart like arrowheads? You clap your hands together, you wring your fingers, you are tormented in your thoughts, you heave some deep and painful groan. The enjoyment of what you have gives you no pleasure; your table is bitter, your countenance [?] gloomy; your ear is ready for any slander against the man who prospers. But if anything good is said of him, your ears are stopped against the words. With your soul in such a state, why do you cloak the disease in hypocrisy? How do you put on the mask of friendship with a show of goodwill? Why do you greet him with friendly and brotherly [?] words, wishing him joy and good health,

while in the secrets of your soul you curse him with the opposite? Such was Cain, who raged at Abel's good repute. Envy within urged him to murder, and pretense became the executioner. Putting on a friendly and affable manner, he led Abel out into the field, far from the protection of their parents, and then revealed his envy by the murder. So whoever drives such a disease out of human life, binds our kind together in goodwill and peace, and leads people into friendly harmony, is he not truly doing a work of divine power? He sets limits to the evils of human nature and brings in their place a sharing in good things. That is why the Lord calls the peacemaker a son of God: he becomes an imitator of the true God, who grants these things to human life. "Blessed, then, are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God." Who are these? The imitators of God's love for humanity, who show in their own lives what is proper to the divine activity. The Lord and Benefactor of good things utterly does away with everything that is alien and foreign to the good, and reduces it to non-existence. He lays down this same activity as a law for you too: to drive out hatred, to end war, to abolish envy, to banish strife, to remove hypocrisy, to quench the resentment smoldering within the heart, and in their place to bring in whatever stands opposite to the things removed. As light comes when darkness withdraws, so in place of each of these the fruit of the Spirit enters: love, joy, peace, kindness, patience, the whole list of good things set out by the Apostle. How, then, is he not blessed who distributes divine gifts, who imitates the graces of God, who makes his own good deeds like the divine generosity? But perhaps the beatitude does not look only to the good of others. I think the one who is properly called a peacemaker is he who brings into peaceful harmony the strife within himself between flesh and spirit, the civil war of our nature. This happens when the law of the body, which wars against the law of the mind, is no longer active, but is yoked under the better rule and becomes a servant of the divine commands. Or rather, let us not suppose that the saying advises us to think of the life of those who have lived rightly as a pair. Instead, once the dividing wall of evil that fences us off within is taken away, the two grow together in a blending with the better and become one. Since the divine is believed to be simple, uncompounded, and without shape, when human nature too, through such peacemaking, leaves behind its double composition and returns exactly to the good, becoming simple and without shape and truly one, so that what is seen is the same as what is hidden and what is hidden the same as what is seen, then the beatitude is truly fulfilled, and [?]

"Blessed are those who have been persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." The order of this lofty teaching brings our present study of the saying to the eighth step. But I think it is right first to consider in our discussion what the mystery of the eighth is in the Prophet, which stands at the head of two psalms, and what the purification and the law of circumcision mean, since the law observes both on the eighth day. Perhaps this number has some kinship with the eighth beatitude, which, like the summit of all the beatitudes, stands at the very top of the good ascent. There the Prophet signifies the day of resurrection by the riddle of the eighth. The purification points to the return of defiled man to his pure and natural state. Circumcision signifies the casting off of the dead skins that we put on when we were stripped of life after the disobedience. And here the eighth beatitude contains the restoration to heaven of those who had fallen into slavery but have been called back from slavery to kingship. For he says, "Blessed are those who have been persecuted for my sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven." See the goal of the contests undertaken for God, the reward for toil, the prize for sweat: to be counted worthy of the kingdom in the heavens. No longer does the hope of good fortune wander among things that are unstable and changing. The earthly region belongs to things that turn and change. But of the things seen and moving in the heavens, we know none that does not remain constant and always the same; everything in the heavens runs its own course in sequence, order, and succession. Do you see, then, how surpassing the gift is? He does not grant this great dignity among changing things, where some fear of change might trouble our better hopes. By saying "the kingdom of heaven," he shows that the gift set before us in hope is unchangeable and always the same. But what I find puzzling in what has been said is this. First, he assigns the same reward both to being poor in spirit and to those persecuted for his sake, giving the two an equal prize. Where the prize is the same, clearly the contests too are equal. Second, how is it that, after separating those on the right from those on the left, he summons them to the kingdom of heaven while naming other reasons for this honor? For there he brings forward compassion, generosity, and love for one another, and nowhere mentions either the [?]

…of [spiritual?] poverty, nor of the persecution for his sake. Yet at first glance these seem very different from one another. What does being poor have in common with being persecuted? And what agreement do these, in turn, have with the [?] of loving compassion? Someone feeds the needy, or clothes the naked, or welcomes a traveller under his roof, or brings whatever care he can to the sick and the imprisoned. As far as the nature of the practice goes, what do these things have in common with being poor and being persecuted? This person heals the misfortunes of others, while each of the other two, the poor man and the persecuted man, is in need of people to care for them. Yet the end is the same for all. He leads to heaven alike the one who has been poor in spirit, the one who has been persecuted for his sake, and those who have shown compassion toward their own kind. What, then, do we say to this? That all these things hold together, converging and breathing in harmony toward one goal. For poverty makes it easy to move on, and love of the poor is no stranger to poverty. But I think it best first to examine the present saying, and only then to consider the harmony and meaning of what has been examined.

“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake.” Persecuted from where, and by whom? The obvious sense points us to the stadium of the martyrs and suggests the race of faith. [?] being pursued [?] expresses the effort of one running at speed, or rather it suggests victory in the race. For [there is no?] other way for a runner to win than by leaving his fellow runner behind him. Now the one who runs toward the prize of the upward call, and the one who is pursued by the enemy on account of the prize, both alike have someone at their back: the first his rival, the second his pursuer. These are the ones who complete the course of martyrdom in the contests for true religion, pursued and not overtaken. So it seems that he has set the culmination of the blessedness laid up in hope, like a kind of crown, in these final words. For it is truly blessed to be persecuted for the Lord’s sake. Why? Because to be driven out by evil becomes the cause of coming to be in the good. Estrangement from the wicked becomes the occasion of closeness to the good; and the good, beyond every good, is the Lord himself, to whom the one who is pursued runs back. Truly blessed, then, is the one who uses the enemy as a fellow worker toward the good. Since human life lies on the border between the good and the worse, just as the one who slips from good and lofty hope ends up in the pit, so the one who is removed from sin and estranged from corruption goes on to righteousness and incorruption. So in the persecution that tyrants bring upon the martyrs, the outward form, as it immediately appears, is painful to the senses, but the purpose of

what happens surpasses all blessedness. [?] It would be [well?] for us to see the meaning of the saying through examples. Who does not know how much harder it is judged to be plotted against than to be loved? And yet what seems hard often becomes for many the cause of good fortune even in this life, as the story of Joseph shows. Plotted against by his brothers and driven from their company, he was through being sold revealed as king over those who had plotted against him. He might perhaps never have risen to so great a rank if envy had not paved the way to kingship through that plot. Suppose someone who knew the future had told Joseph beforehand, “You are blessed in being plotted against.” He would not readily have seemed believable to the hearer, who looked only at the pain of the moment; for he would not have thought it possible for a good end to come out of an evil intention. So it is here too. The persecution brought by tyrants upon the faithful, which carries much pain to the senses, makes it hard for the more carnal to accept the hope of the kingdom laid before them through sufferings. But the Lord, regarding the frailty of our nature, announces in advance to the weaker [?] what the end of the contest is, so that by the hope of the kingdom they may easily wrestle down the passing sensation of pain. This is why the great Stephen rejoices as he is stoned on every side, and eagerly receives on his body the thick showers of stones as if they were a sweet dew, and [repays?] those [who were killing him?] with blessings, praying for these very men [?], since he had [heard?] the promise [?] and [saw] the hope coinciding with what appeared [?]. For having heard that those persecuted for the Lord’s sake come to be in the kingdom of heaven, he [saw?] what he was looking for, the very thing for which he was being pursued. For to the one who [runs?] through confession, what is hoped for is shown: heaven opened, divine glory [looking down?] upon the contest of the runner from the realm above the world, [?] he himself who in the contests is [confessed?] by the athlete. For the standing of the president of the games signals in a riddle his alliance with the one contending, so that through this we might learn that the same one both sets the contests and stands with his own contestants against their opponents. What, then, could be more blessed than the one persecuted for the Lord’s sake, who will have the president of the games as his fellow contestant? For it is no easy thing, and perhaps altogether impossible, to prefer the good that is not seen to the pleasant things of this life that are seen, so that one readily chooses to be [driven from?] his house, or to be parted from wife and children, brothers and parents and companions, and all the pleasures of life, unless the Lord himself works together for good with the one who has been called according to his purpose. For whom he foreknows, as the Apostle says, him

he also predestines, and calls, and justifies, and glorifies. Now the soul somehow grows into the pleasures of life through the bodily senses. It delights in the bright colours of matter through the eyes; through hearing it is inclined toward pleasant sounds; and with smell, taste and touch it is disposed according to what is natural to each. For this reason, fastened to the pleasures of life by its power of sensation as if by a nail, it is hard to tear away from the things it has grown attached to. Like tortoises and snails, bound up in a kind of shell, it moves only with difficulty toward such motions, dragging the whole burden of life along with it. So a soul in this state is easily caught by its persecutors when they threaten confiscation, or a fine, or the loss of anything else people prize in this life; it readily gives in and falls into the persecutor’s hands. But when the living Word, as the Apostle says, active and sharper than any two-edged sword, enters the one who has truly received the faith, and cuts apart what had wrongly grown together, and severs the bonds of habit, then the soul shakes off worldly pleasures like a burden tied to it, as a runner shakes a load from his shoulders, and light and unencumbered it runs the course of the contests, with the president of the games himself to lead it by the hand along the track. It does not look at what it has left behind but at what it is pursuing. It does not turn its eye back to the pleasure behind it but presses on toward the good set before it. It is not pained by the loss of earthly things but [rejoices?] in the gain of heavenly ones. Therefore it readily accepts every kind of punishment as an occasion and aid toward the joy set before it: fire as a cleansing of matter; the sword as cutting the mind away from its fusion with material and fleshly things; every form of toil and pain it eagerly accepts as an antidote to the evil poison of pleasure. Just as people who suffer from excess humours and bile readily drink a bitter remedy so that the cause of their illness may be washed out, so the one who is pursued by the enemy and flees to God accepts the onset of pain as something that quenches the working of pleasure; for one who is in pain cannot feel pleasure. Since, then, sin entered through pleasure, it will surely be driven out by its opposite. So those who persecute for the sake of confessing the Lord, and devise unbearable punishments, are in fact applying a kind of medicine to souls through suffering, treating the disease of pleasure with the assaults of pain. In this way Paul accepts the cross, James the sword, Stephen the stones, the blessed Peter crucifixion head downward; and all the contestants of the faith after them accepted the many kinds of punishment: wild beasts, pits, pyres, freezing in the cold, the stripping of flesh from the ribs, the binding round of heads, the [gouging out?] of eyes,

what happens surpasses all blessedness. [?] looking at the pain of the moment. What, then, could be more blessed than the one persecuted for the Lord’s sake, who has the president of the games as his fellow contestant? For it is no easy thing, and perhaps altogether impossible, to prefer the good that is not seen to the pleasant things of this life that are seen, so that one readily chooses to be driven from his house, or to be parted from wife and children, brothers and parents and companions, and all the pleasures of life, unless the Lord himself works together for good with the one who has been called according to his purpose. For whom he foreknows, as the Apostle says, him

[gougings out?], the cutting off of fingers, the tearing apart of the body by the legs, the wasting away of hunger. All these and the like the saints welcomed with gladness as cleansings from sin, so that no trace [?] that had arisen through [?] might remain, since the sharp and painful sensation [?] wipes away all the impressions that pleasure has left in the soul. Blessed, then, are those persecuted for my sake. To understand the other sense as well, this is as if one were to give speech to health; it too would say, “Blessed are those separated from [sickness] for my sake.” For estrangement from what is grievous brings those who were once sick to be in me. Let us hear the voice in this way, as though life itself were crying out this beatitude to us: “Blessed are those pursued by death for my sake.” Or as if light were to say, “Blessed are those pursued by darkness for my sake.” So too righteousness, and holiness, and incorruption, and goodness, and every idea of what is thought and spoken of as better. The Lord, being [?], is to be thought of as saying to you in that sense: “Blessed is everyone who is driven away from every contrary thing: corruption, darkness, sin, injustice, [?], and each of the things and ideas set apart from the principles of virtue.” For to come to be outside evils is to be established within good things. “Whoever commits sin,” says [?], “is a slave of sin.” So the one who has left what he served is raised to the dignity of freedom. The highest form of freedom is to become one’s own master; and the rank of kingship has no tyranny set above it. If, then, the one who is estranged from sin is his own master, and it is proper to kingship to be self-governing and subject to no lord, it follows that the one driven away from evil is called blessed, since being driven from there procures for him the royal dignity. Let us not be grieved, then, brothers, when we are driven away from earthly things. For he who moves away from here takes up his dwelling in the royal palaces of heaven. There are these two elements in the creation of things, apportioned for the life of rational nature: earth and heaven. Earth is the place of those whose lot it is to live through the flesh, heaven the place of the bodiless. Our life must therefore be somewhere. If we are not driven from the earth, we shall certainly remain on the earth; if we depart from here, we shall be moved to heaven. Do you see where the beatitude leads, becoming for you the cause of so great a good through what seems grievous? Understanding this, the Apostle also says: “All discipline seems for the present to be a matter not of joy but of sorrow; but afterward it [yields] the peaceful fruit to those who have been trained by it,

[?] of righteousness.” Affliction, then, is the flower of the fruits we hope for. For the sake of the fruit, then, let us pluck the flower too. Let us be pursued so that we may run; and when we run, we shall not run aimlessly, but let our race be toward the prize of the upward call. Let us so run that we may obtain. What is it we obtain? What is the prize? What is the crown? To me it seems that each of the things we hope for is nothing other than the Lord himself. For he is both the president of the games for those who compete and the crown of those who win. He is the one who distributes the inheritance; he is the good inheritance. He is the good portion; he is the one who grants you the portion. He is the one who makes rich; he is the wealth. He shows you the treasure and becomes your treasure. He leads you to desire the beautiful pearl, and is offered for sale to you if you trade well. So, in order to acquire that, let us, as in a market, exchange what we have for what we do not have. Let us not be grieved, then, when we are persecuted, but rather let us be glad, because by being driven from what is valued on earth we are herded together toward the heavenly good, according to him who promised that those persecuted for his sake are blessed, “for theirs is the kingdom of heaven,” by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, for to him belong the glory and the power to the ages of ages. Amen.
